news.title: AOC, Donald Trump Jr. Make Gains in New 2028 Poll
news.text: Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Donald Trump Jr. gained ground among voters considering potential 2028 presidential contenders in a new Harvard CAPS/Harris poll, while the leaders of the hypothetical Democratic and Republican fields saw their support slip. The shifts offer an early look at a 2028 race that is still taking shape, with none of the potential contenders tested in the poll having formally announced a campaign. Among Democrats, former Vice President Kamala Harris remains the leading choice at 38 percent, down 4 percentage points from August. California Governor Gavin Newsom followed at 17 percent, while Ocasio-Cortez climbed 3 points to 12 percent. Ocasio-Cortez has not yet decided whether she will run for president in 2028, saying she plans to weigh the decision after the midterm elections. In an interview with The New York Times published last week, Ocasio-Cortez discussed the challenges of a potential presidential campaign. “This country has never elected a female president. Why are we pretending that this is not a factor?” Ocasio-Cortez told the Times. “That doesn’t make it impossible, but to act as though it’s not a factor in anything ever is really a form of, like, denialism.” On the Republican side, Vice President JD Vance remained in first place at 39 percent in the poll, down 3 points from August. Trump Jr. jumped 6 points to 24 percent, followed by Marco Rubio at 17 percent. Trump Jr. has previously left open the possibility of a presidential run, but has also said he is not currently interested in running in 2028. ”I've always said, while I'll never 100% rule it out down the line, I have ZERO interest in running for office in 28 or anytime soon,” Trump Jr. wrote on X in May 2025. The Harvard CAPS/Harris poll was conducted online from September 26 to 28, 2026, among 2,200 registered voters. The survey has a margin of error of approximately plus or minus 2.1 percentage points. Newsweek reached out to representatives for both Ocasio-Cortez and Trump Jr. via email late Tuesday. What Voters Are Saying Ahead of Midterms More immediately, with just 35 days until the November election, the poll also found that 42 percent of voters have not firmly settled on their midterm choice. Twenty-six percent of those surveyed said they are leaning toward certain candidates but could still change their minds, while another 16 percent said they have not yet decided. Fifty percent said they have definitely made up their minds, according to the survey. On the economy, voters were closely divided when asked whether the economy is better or worse than it was when Joe Biden was president. Fifty-three percent said the economy today is worse, compared with 47 percent who said it is better. Among independent voters, 61 percent said the economy is worse today than it was under Biden, while 39 percent said it is better. The economy and inflation continue to top voters' concerns, with 45 percent saying inflation is the issue most important to them personally. Artificial intelligence also emerged as a notable issue, with 15 percent citing it as a top concern. Trump has continued to defend his economic record in recent days, saying the country has the “best economy we've ever had.” “We have the best employment numbers that came out in the history of our country. More people working today than at any time ever before,” Trump told reporters while departing the White House Sunday. He also reiterated that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends, which he said will happen “soon.” The Trump administration is also considering a ban on U.S. diesel exports. Nationwide, drivers are paying an average $4.46 for a regular gallon of gas, and $6.44 for diesel, according to AAA. “With oil holding below $100 per barrel, many Americans may see modest declines ahead for gasoline and slight drops for diesel, but the West Coast faces continued pressure with further increases possible,” Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, said in a statement. “The broader geopolitical situation remains fluid and could push prices in either direction with little warning, and with Trump still weighing a diesel export ban, impacts could follow.” Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: New polling finds Harris and Vance leading their parties while AOC and Trump Jr. make gains.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Chris Cuomo Claims Ex-Prez Joe Biden Privately Admitted He 'Sabotaged' Democrats During 2024 Election: 'He Wanted to Punish Them'
news.text:
Chris Cuomo has claimed former President Joe Biden privately admitted that he "sabotaged" Democrats during the 2024 presidential election after party leaders pushed him to end his reelection campaign, RadarOnline has learned.

The NewsNation host made the claim during the September 24 episode of his podcast, The Chris Cuomo Project, arguing Biden was angry over the effort to replace him on the Democratic ticket and deliberately made the transition more difficult.'I Believe He Screwed Up the Process'Cuomo said people who have heard Biden speak privately told him the former president still acknowledges what he did.

"He was so p--sed that they didn't want him to run again, that I believe he submarined the whole thing,” Cuomo claimed. "I believe he forced (Kamala) Harris on them, I believe he delayed it, I believe he screwed up the process, I believe he wanted to punish them for not letting him run again. I really believe that."

Cuomo’s comments center on the chaotic period after Biden’s June 2024 debate against then-Republican presidential nominee Donald Trump.

Biden faced mounting pressure from Democratic lawmakers following the debate and announced July 21, 2024, that he would end his reelection bid. 

He endorsed then-Vice President Kamala Harris shortly afterward.Kamala Harris and Joe Biden’s Complicated Political RelationshipCuomo argued that Biden’s anger over being pushed aside influenced what happened next.

The journalist claimed Biden remained "very angry" about how Democrats handled the 2024 race and was so "disgusted" that he chose not to vote for Harris.

Cuomo did not provide details explaining how Biden allegedly "forced" Democrats to nominate Harris. He also did not identify the people he said had heard Biden acknowledge the alleged sabotage during private conversations.

Harris’ relationship with Biden became more complicated after the 2024 campaign.

When she inherited the Democratic nomination following his decision to end his reelection bid, during their four years in the White House, Harris publicly defended Biden.Kamala Harris Sounds OffIn a 2024 CNN interview, Harris recalled that Biden personally called her to tell her he had decided to withdraw from the race. "My first thought was not about me, to be honest with you. My first thought was about him," she said.

Her public tone changed after the election. In her memoir, Harris wrote that leaving the decision over Biden's reelection campaign to the former president and first lady Jill Biden was "recklessness," arguing that the stakes were too high for the decision to be treated as a personal matter.

By August 2026, Harris was also openly contrasting her approach with Biden’s earlier belief that Republicans could experience an “epiphany” after Trump left politics, saying Democrats cannot "sit around hoping Republicans will have an 'epiphany' and do the right thing."

Cuomo based his claim about Biden's alleged private admission on conversations with unnamed people who he said had heard the former president discuss the 2024 election.'He Will Still Tell People That He Did It'"He will still tell people that he did it," Cuomo said.

The allegation adds another explanation for one of the most consequential moments of the 2024 presidential campaign, when Biden ended his reelection bid and Harris quickly became the Democratic nominee.

Biden ultimately remained out of the race while Trump defeated Harris in the November election.

Cuomo's account, however, remains an allegation about Biden's private thinking and actions rather than an independently established explanation for the Democrats’ 2024 defeat.
news.summary: Chris Cuomo claims Joe Biden privately admitted to sabotaging Democrats in 2024 after party leaders pushed him out of the presidential race.
news.author: Christian Spencer

news.title: MS NOW star Molly Jong-Fast jokingly DEFENDS Trump after President, 80, appeared to nod off moments after attacking 'Sleepy Joe' Biden
news.text:
MS NOW commentator Molly Jong-Fast offered a sarcastic defense of Donald Trump after the President was roundly accused of falling asleep during a White House event on Monday.

The 2pm event was held to announce plans to bring a $15 billion steel mill to Iowa. 

Jong-Fast, 48, reacted to one of many clips showing Trump, 80, with his eyes closed at the event.

Riffing off the fact that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had been stressing the importance of domestic steel production in the clip, Jong-Fast quipped on X: 'In trumps defense howard is very very boring.'

The 14 seconds of footage, shared by Kamala Harris's rebooted 2024 campaign X account, came from a longer White House feed where Trump is seen repeatedly reopening his eyes and speaking to attendees.

Politicians and commentators were still quick to accuse the conservative of falling asleep.

Trump also once again revived his sleep-related nickname for his predecessor, Joe Biden, during the Oval Office meeting, leading to a jab from his son, Hunter. 

'Sleepy who?' he wrote over an unflattering still of the President.

California Governor Gavin Newsom also got his licks in, via a post from his press office.

'President McConnell is looking great,' the office wrote on X, an off-color reference to 84-year-old Senator Mitch McConnell's recent health struggles. 

'I have no doubt in my mind that Donald Trump fell asleep multiple times today. He’s just tired, just like we’re all tired of him,' liberal commentator Brian Krassenstein wrote.

Aaron Rupar wrote: 'Trump is struggling to stay awake on camera.' 

The barb from Jong-Fast was only the latest from the cable news star this month to cast doubt on Trump's mental faculties, after Biden ended up abandoning his 2024 reelection run just months before the election.

'So sleepy,' the daughter of feminist author Erica Jong wrote in a Threads post published on September 18, in reaction to a post from the account 'DemsMight' with footage of a tired-looking Trump with his eyes closed at an event earlier in the day. 

A caption panned the conservative as 'an embarrassment.' 

After critics accused Trump of falling asleep at a Washington, DC, 9/11 ceremony, Jong-Fast wrote on X: 'It’s weird that the president keeps falling asleep in the middle of the day, but it’s even weirder that this isn’t more of a scandal.

'But what do I know I’ve been worrying about climate change this whole time when I should have been worried about an AI apocalypse,' the post continued.

When Rupar shared a clip of Trump with his eyes closed during an event in the Oval Office with travel industry executives the day before back on September 2, Jong-Fast took to Threads to proclaim: 'Is anyone worried that the president can’t stay awake?'

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle proclaimed: 'Anyone claiming the President was asleep is lying,' when approached for comment Tuesday by the Daily Mail

'President Trump’s sharpness, unmatched energy, and historic accessibility stand in stark contrast to what we saw during the last administration when Democrats and the legacy media intentionally covered up Joe Biden’s serious mental and physical decline from the American people,' Ingle said in a statement.

'President Trump is the sharpest and most accessible President in American history who is working nonstop to solve problems and deliver on his promises, and he remains in excellent health.'

Jong-Fast runs a political podcast, Fast Politics with Molly Jong-Fast, in addition to her MS NOW duties.

Her expertise lies in Washington, but she wrote an op-ed for The New York Times last month surrounding the stigma female patients face when undergoing plastic surgeries. 

She detailed her recent decision to get a face- and neck-lift in the piece. 

'My face, for instance, is directly connected to my livelihood,' she wrote at a point, noting that she discusses 'politics on TV for a living.'

'What I did to my face isn’t that unusual; I’d argue that it’s actually the norm for women on TV these days.'

She released a memoir surrounding her upbringing under her 84-year-old mother early last year. The book painted the pair's relationship as 'complicated' and one that 'can really mess you up.
news.summary: The 2pm event where Trump was filmed with his eyes closed for a prolonged period surrounded plans to bring a $15 billion steel mill to Iowa.
news.author: Alex Hammer,Editor

news.title: We Asked Trump's New AI Government Site About His Controversial Claims
news.text: The Trump administration's newly launched America.gov chatbot provided direct answers Tuesday to a series of questions about the 2020 election, presidential term limits, impeachment proceedings and other politically sensitive topics when Newsweek tested the system shortly after its debut. The administration has promoted the AI-powered platform as a tool that draws information from official government sources and could become a public-facing gateway to federal information. The answers could also intensify scrutiny over how government AI systems handle politically sensitive subjects as federal agencies increasingly deploy artificial intelligence tools. Newsweek submitted 15 prompts to the chatbot between 12:54 p.m. and 1:06 p.m. ET, asking about election results, alleged election fraud, climate science, presidential salaries, impeachment history, criminal convictions and Trump's eligibility to seek a third term. In each case reviewed by Newsweek, the chatbot cited government records, constitutional provisions, federal agencies or other official sources as the basis for its answer. Newsweek has reached out to the White House for comment. Trump's New AI Government Website: What to Know America.gov is designed to pull information from federal agencies and present it through a chatbot-style interface. Rather than searching separate government websites, users can enter questions or requests and receive answers sourced from official government information. Officials compared the experience to consumer AI platforms, saying that the system is intended to guide users through government processes and explain requirements for services such as Medicare enrollment, disaster assistance and federal job applications. The current version is primarily focused on providing information and helping users find answers. It can explain procedures and direct users to relevant resources, but it cannot yet complete many government transactions on a user's behalf. Who Won the 2020 Presidential Election? At 12:54 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked the chatbot: "Who won the 2020 presidential election?" The system answered, "Joseph R. Biden Jr. won the 2020 U.S. presidential election," citing Electoral College results showing Biden received 306 electoral votes to Donald Trump's 232. It also linked to National Archives records and Federal Election Commission results. The chatbot delivered the same conclusion when Newsweek returned to the topic later in the testing period. Asked again twice at 1:01 p.m. "Who lost the 2020 presidential election?" and "Did Donald Trump lose the 2020 election?" it again answered that Biden won and cited the same records. Was There Widespread Fraud That Changed the Result of the 2020 Election? At 12:55 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Was there widespread fraud that changed the result of the 2020 election?" The chatbot responded: "Official U.S. government sources did not find widespread fraud that changed the 2020 presidential election result." It cited findings from federal agencies, election officials and intelligence reviews and stated that while isolated irregularities can occur, official reviews and recounts did not identify fraud on a scale that altered the outcome. Can Donald Trump Run for President in 2028? At 12:56 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Can Donald Trump run for president in 2028?" The chatbot answered: "No. Under the 22nd Amendment, no person may be elected President more than twice. Donald Trump has already been elected President twice (2016 and 2024), so he cannot be elected again in 2028." It added that another election victory would require a constitutional amendment changing the existing term-limit provision and cited the text of the Constitution's 22nd Amendment. The chatbot also noted that it was not providing legal advice. What Federal Department Is Headquartered at the Pentagon? At 12:57 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "What federal department is headquartered at the Pentagon?" The chatbot answered: "The Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, is the headquarters of the Department of War (formerly the Department of Defense)." The response cited military installation information and referenced Trump's Executive Order 14347, which it said authorized "Department of War" as a secondary title for the Department of Defense. The department's legal name remains the Department of Defense. While Executive Order 14347 authorized the use of "Department of War" as a secondary designation, Congress has not changed the agency's statutory name, meaning the Pentagon remains the headquarters of the Department of Defense under federal law. Is Recent Climate Change Primarily Caused by Human Activity? Also at 12:57 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Is recent climate change primarily caused by human activity?" The chatbot responded: "Official U.S. sources do not all state the same conclusion. "Many longstanding agency science pages say recent warming is mainly from human greenhouse-gas emissions (especially fossil fuels), not natural causes alone," it said. It also cited NOAA and the Environmental Protection Agency before adding: "A July 2025 Department of Energy report (Climate Working Group assembled by the Energy Secretary) says climate has always changed naturally; human CO₂ is a warming influence, but it emphasizes uncertainties, aerosol cooling, and that CO₂-driven warming may be less economically damaging than often claimed. "Climate has varied naturally for Earth’s history. How much of recent change is human-caused is a scientific attribution question; agencies currently present both the traditional assessment and this newer DOE review. I do not offer political commentary." Was Donald Trump the First President to Decline His Salary? At 12:58 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Was Donald Trump the first president to decline his salary?" "No," the bot answered. "Donald Trump was not the first president to decline or give away the presidential salary." The bot went on to cite the Herbert Hoover Presidential Library to say that Hoover did "not keep his federal salary as president (or in earlier federal posts); he put it toward staff supplements and charity." It also said: "John F. Kennedy also did not keep the presidential salary, according to the same Hoover Library post." Finally, it added George Washington to the mix, saying that the first U.S. president "would serve without pay; Congress still set a salary of $25,000." The response also noted that Trump donated his salary during his first term. It ended by saying: "The Constitution still requires a presidential salary that cannot be changed during a term. I do not give legal advice." Has Donald Trump Been Impeached? At 12:58 p.m. ET, the chatbot answered yes when asked: "Has Donald Trump been impeached?" "The House of Representatives impeached Donald Trump twice. The Senate did not convict him either time," the bot said. The system identified the first impeachment in 2019 and the second in 2021 and cited congressional records, then added: "Impeachment by the House is a formal charge. Removal requires a two-thirds Senate vote to convict. I do not offer legal or political commentary." Has Donald Trump Been Convicted of Felony Charges? At 12:59 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Has Donald Trump been convicted of felony charges?" The chatbot answered, "Yes, on a New York state jury verdict." "On May 30, 2024, a New York County jury found Donald Trump guilty of 34 counts of falsifying business records in the first degree (a felony under New York Penal Law § 175.10). "That is a state criminal case, not a federal conviction. Later sentencing, appeals, or other court action can change what happens after a verdict; I cannot give legal advice." The bot also included sources linking out to the New York Courts decision, People v. Trump 2024 NY Slip Op, and the case docket. Who Was Inaugurated as President on January 20, 2021? At 1:02 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Who was inaugurated as president on January 20, 2021?" The chatbot answered: "Joseph R. Biden Jr. was inaugurated as the 46th President of the United States on January 20, 2021." It also noted that Kamala Harris was sworn in as vice president during the same ceremony and cited congressional inauguration records. The bot added a link to the Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies to support its response. What Were the Certified Electoral College Results in 2020? Newsweek asked the bot at 1:02 p.m. ET: "What were the certified Electoral College results in 2020?" The chatbot replied, "Certified 2020 Electoral College results (538 electors; 270 needed to win): "Vice President: Kamala D. Harris 306, Michael R. Pence 232. The response cited National Archives records and presented the figures without additional commentary. Has a President Ever Been Impeached Twice? When Newsweek posed this question at 1:02 p.m. ET, the chatbot answered yes and stated that Trump is the only U.S. president to have been impeached twice. The system referenced the 2019 and 2021 impeachment proceedings and cited congressional records for its answer. Similarly, at 1:03 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked a variation of the impeachment question: "How many times was Donald Trump impeached? The chatbot's answer was, "Twice. "The House of Representatives impeached Donald Trump in 2019 and again in 2021. The Senate did not convict him either time." Who Lost the 2020 Presidential Election? At 1:05 p.m. ET, Newsweek asked: "Who lost the 2020 presidential election?" The chatbot responded: "Donald J. Trump lost the 2020 U.S. presidential election. "Electoral College: Trump 232, Joseph R. Biden Jr. 306 (270 needed to win). The answer was consistent with several earlier election-related responses generated during Newsweek's testing period. At 1:06 p.m. ET, Newsweek rephrased the question one final time: "Did Donald Trump lose the 2020 election?" The chatbot again answered, "Yes. Donald J. Trump lost the 2020 presidential election." It also cited the official Electoral College tally. Across multiple election-related prompts, including questions about the winner, loser, inauguration and Electoral College certification, the chatbot consistently relied on federal election records and government sources, and responded accurately. Trump's Stance on AI Trump used the rollout to reinforce his administration's support for artificial intelligence development. While concerns about AI safety, cybersecurity and misuse have intensified in recent years, Trump argued that the United States should continue pushing ahead with the technology rather than slowing development. The launch took place just hours before Trump was scheduled to meet with technology executives to discuss AI-related issues, including growing concerns about security breaches and risks associated with advanced systems. Administration officials have increasingly framed AI as both an economic and national competitiveness issue, arguing that the U.S. must continue investing in the technology to remain ahead of international rivals. Additionally, Trump declared at the United Nations last Tuesday that the U.S. government would replace “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” in official documents. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gabe Whisnant and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: President Donald Trump says AI can improve government services as America.gov rolls out ahead of a broader 2027 expansion.
news.author: Amanda Castro

news.title: Trump to Campaign in Nebraska as GOP Faces Close Senate Race in Red State
news.text: President Donald Trump is campaigning in Nebraska next week, as Republican Senator Pete Ricketts faces a competitive challenge from independent Dan Osborn in the traditionally conservative state. Nebraska backed Trump by more than 20 points in the 2024 election, so it is not the kind of state that would ordinarily be seen as competitive. But the race is viewed as tighter than the GOP would like ahead of November's midterm elections. Osborn, a labor leader who has said he would not caucus with either party if elected, is viewed as a uniquely strong candidate after his showing in the 2024 Senate race against Republican Senator Deb Fischer. His 7-point loss was seen as an overperformance given the state’s Republican voting record and Trump’s significant victory on the same ticket. Republicans are also facing tougher headwinds this year, as Trump’s national approval rating has fallen due to voter frustration with the economy, cost of living and gas prices as a result of the continuing war with Iran. Historically, when the president is unpopular, his party suffers losses in the midterms, and Democrats have sought to make this year's elections a referendum on Trump. Trump is set to campaign in Grand Island on Monday. Republican National Committee spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre told Newsweek the president “looks forward to rallying in support of Senator Pete Ricketts, a proven business leader and public servant who will always put Nebraskans first.” She noted that Trump “will be barnstorming the country ahead of the midterms.” The rally is set to be held at Nebraska State Fair's Pinnacle Bank Expo Center, and doors will open at 2:30 p.m., according to The Omaha World Herald. Trump is expected to speak at about 6 p.m., the newspaper reported. It comes as Republicans try to avert losses in the midterms, as polling suggests their majorities in the House and Senate are at risk. An Osborn victory in Nebraska would complicate their path to holding onto the majority, so the GOP is working to motivate their base to ensure Ricketts holds onto the seat. Newsweek reached out to the Ricketts campaign for comment via email. Trump Nebraska Rally Is ‘Tough’ Sign for GOP The rally could help Ricketts “energize the Republican base and motivate them to go out and vote,” Kevin Smith, a political scientist at the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, told Newsweek on Tuesday. The fact that Trump is in Nebraska campaigning for an incumbent conservative member of the GOP is “perhaps a sign of a tough electoral environment for Republicans,” he said. “A Republican running in a ruby red state like Nebraska should be a layup, not something that requires an all-hands-on-deck push by party leaders to secure the win.” The rally is the second recently announced event for Trump in a solidly conservative state. He is also set to appear in Durant, Oklahoma, on October 1. Oklahoma is even more conservative than Nebraska, giving Trump a 34-point victory in 2024. Dan Osborn Responds Osborn responded to the announcement in a statement to Newsweek, saying that Ricketts is “begging the party bosses to come save this election for him. “In 2024 the president campaigned on no forever wars, standing up to China, lowering the cost of groceries, and securing the border. I’m still running on that same platform two years later. Ricketts has abandoned those principles,” he wrote. Pete Ricketts vs. Dan Osborn: What Polls Show Polling of the Nebraska Senate race is limited, and most of the public surveys are Osborn internals. A SurveyUSA poll gave Osborn a 4-point lead, 46 percent to 42 percent, with 4 percent preferring another candidate and 7 percent being undecided. It surveyed 503 likely voters September 8-13. Osborn and Ricketts were tied in a recent poll from Impact Research, a Democratic polling firm. They each received 47 percent support in the poll, which surveyed 600 likely voters August 9-13. A Tavern Research poll from May showed Osborn with a 5-point lead over Ricketts, 47 percent to 42 percent. It surveyed 1,165 likely voters May 8-11 and had a margin of error of ±3.5 percentage points. There is no Democratic candidate in the race. Democrats in the state have largely coalesced around Osborn’s candidacy. Smith said the race is more competitive than he expected it to be. “Osborn was always expected to perform decently given his result against Fischer, but the massive party registration advantage for Republicans would have made anyone reluctant to bet against Ricketts six or seven months ago,” he said. “If those polls are in the ballpark, though, this is certainly closer than I expected and Osborn’s chances as a dark horse seem more real with every poll that's come out.” Ricketts, a former governor, was appointed to the seat after former Senator Ben Sasse resigned to become president of the University of Florida in 2023. He won a special election in 2024 and is now seeking a full term. Nebraska House Races Nebraska’s Second Congressional District is one of the most closely watched House races of the midterms and could be a bellwether for how the nation votes as a whole. The district, based around Omaha, is represented by Republican Don Bacon, though it narrowly backed Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. Bacon is retiring, leaving open a key seat. Democrat Denise Powell, co-founder of the group Women Who Run, is running against Republican Brinker Harding, an Omaha city council member. The SurveyUSA poll gave Powell a 4-point lead, 46 percent to 42 percent. The Cook Political Report classifies it as Lean Democratic. Nebraska’s First District, which backed Trump by 13 points, has also garnered some national attention. Republican Representative Mike Flood is facing a challenge from Democrat Chris Backemeyer, who served as the deputy assistant secretary of state during the Biden administration. That race is considered Solid Republican by Cook, which noted that it would "take a combination of high turnout in Lincoln and anemic turnout in the surrounding rural counties for Flood to have another competitive race." Smith said that Flood is a “pro and a good politician” who has a “long and respected track record at the state as well as national levels.” “I still think he's in the drivers seat in that race, but I'm getting the sense this is going to be a more competitive race than it has been in the past,” he said. Dan Osborn’s Independent Pitch Osborn has cast himself as a true independent who aligns with neither party on all issues. He told CNN in August that if elected, he does not plan to caucus with either party. “I plan on remaining an independent,” he said. However, Republicans have sought to cast doubt on his independence. They have pointed to past remarks made by Osborn, including that Trump’s wall along the U.S.-Mexico border is a “symbol of racism,” to tie him to Democrats, who are not popular in the state. “Democrat Dan Osborn is a grifter who wants to raise taxes on Nebraska families and work with the radical left to open our borders. Nebraskans will reject Osborn again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee regional press secretary Nick Puglia said in a statement in July. Osborn faces a tough climb in Nebraska, where Republicans hold a substantial advantage on the voter rolls. As of September, there were 619,984 registered Republicans and 327,935 registered Democrats across Nebraska. There were only 282,473 people who are nonpartisan and 28,277 Nebraskans registered with other parties, according to registration numbers from the Nebraska Secretary of State's Office. The state backed Trump in all three of his presidential runs, though his margins were narrower than Republican victories earlier in the century. Trump won Nebraska by just over 20 points in 2024 after winning it by 19 points in 2020 and 25 in 2016. The state also voted for Republicans by 22 points in 2012, 15 points in 2008, 33 points in 2004 and 29 points in 2000. Democrats haven’t carried the state presidentially since 1964. Nebraska’s vast, rural regions keep the state Republican, despite a few blue dots in cities such as Omaha and Lincoln. Issues such as rising diesel prices and Trump’s plan to import foreign beef could be shaping the Senate race in Nebraska, which has a large agricultural industry. “The Nebraska cattlemen were not happy about the beef imports, and high fuel costs and their connection to the war in Iran is a bipartisan concern,” Smith said. What Happens Next Nebraska’s Senate race is going to be closely watched as both parties compete for control of the Senate. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to secure a majority because Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in a 50-50 Senate. An Osborn victory in Nebraska would make it easier for them to flip Congress' upper chamber by denying Republicans a seat in a solidly conservative state. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Samantha Beech and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: President Trump campaigning in such a conservative state may be a "tough" sign for Republicans, one politics expert told Newsweek.
news.author: Andrew Stanton

news.title: David Crowley welcomes campaigning with Kamala Harris, Francesca Hong
news.text:
Democratic candidate David Crowley said Tuesday he is open to campaigning with former Vice President Kamala Harris and former primary opponent Francesca Hong.

Crowley told reporters at a campaign event Sept. 29 in Milwaukee he is willing to campaign with "anybody who's willing to focus on lowering costs for working families," including Harris, who lost the 2024 presidential election in Wisconsin, and Hong, a democratic socialist who narrowly lost the primary to Crowley.

"At the end of the day, this is about making sure that we don't have a MAGA extremist occupying our governor's office ... somebody who voted to give millions of dollars in tax breaks to billionaires while working families struggle each and every single day," Crowley said of Republican opponent Tom Tiffany, a congressman representing the 7th U.S. House district.

"If you believe that this is the campaign that you should be supporting because you believe in the ideas and the values and the mission that we need here in the state of Wisconsin, I welcome anyone to be a part of this."

A spokeswoman for Tiffany said, "David Crowley’s decision to fly across the country to fundraise with Kamala Harris while asking Francesca Hong to campaign with him tells Wisconsinites everything they need to know."

"David Crowley is embracing an agenda of open borders, socialist policies, higher taxes, and bigger government that would leave Wisconsin taxpayers paying the price."

Crowley's comments come a day after Harris held a high-dollar fundraiser for Crowley in Santa Monica, California and after Hong began touring the state to campaign for Democrats.

Hong lost to Crowley by less than one percentage point. Crowley and Hong each received more than 300,000 votes after a chaotic last month of the primary during which Crowley dropped out and reentered the race with the endorsement of Gov. Tony Evers − a move criticized by some Democrats, including Hong supporters, as a party establishment power grab.

Since then, Crowley has sought to win over support from Hong's supporters.

In an interview with WISN, Hong said "it's important that David lets our supporters know that he shares our values."

She later told supporters at an event in Milwaukee to not write her in on November's ballot.

"I’m not out here to tell you what to do. But I do got to say, please do not write me in or vote for me. I’m no longer a candidate," Hong said Sept. 26.
news.author: Journal Sentinel

news.title: Trump to Return to the Lone Star State for Second Time This Month
news.text:
President Donald Trump will be visiting Texas on Thursday to tout Peterbilt Motors in the backdrop of competitive midterm races in the Lone Star State, according to Fox Business on Tuesday. 

“President Trump will visit Peterbilt Motors in Denton, Texas, on Thursday to tout his pro-growth economic agenda that has created more than one million private-sector jobs, sparked trillions in new investments, lowered taxes, and re-shored key manufacturing back to the United States,” White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales said in a statement. 

“The President’s America First trade agenda is driving a manufacturing renaissance that will continue paying dividends for the great state of Texas and Americans across the country,” Wales continued.

news.title: A Kansas Democrat’s red-state pitch: A two-term limit and no Trump trials
news.text:
WICHITA, Kan. — Adam Hamilton doesn’t plan to stay in Washington long if he gets there, and he doesn’t plan to spend his time investigating President Donald Trump.

The 62-year-old megachurch pastor, running a surprisingly competitive Senate campaign as a Democrat in Kansas, told MS NOW he would serve no more than two terms in the chamber if elected. He also said he had no interest in the investigations of Trump and his family that Democratic leaders have signaled they would pursue if their party wins control of Congress.

“I’m not going to Washington to hold trials. I’m going to Washington to fight for the people of Kansas and make life better for them,” Hamilton told MS NOW in an interview, adding that Congress must establish “guardrails” to ensure that “some of the things that have happened in the last two years or in the last 12 years don’t happen again.”

Both stances are part of Hamilton's effort to cast himself as a political outsider, and one who intends to stay that way even after arriving on Capitol Hill.

Hamilton favors term limits — “no more than 18 years of service, combined, House, Senate, White House” — and said he would hold himself to a stricter standard, leaving Congress after no more than 12 years.

“I’m going in as though I'm going to be there for six years, and I'm going to do all the good I can in those six years,” he told MS NOW. “If you go in and you're thinking, ‘I don't care if I get re-elected, I want to fight for the American people and do what's best,’ I may not be there after six years, and that's OK with me.”

“And if I felt like I could make a difference, maybe there’s six more years,” he added. “That’s it.”

Hamilton's nonpartisan pitch appears to be resonating in a state where only a quarter of voters are Democrats and that hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate in almost a century. Amid a national wave of discontent with the GOP, polls show him in a tight race with incumbent Republican Sen. Roger Marshall, and the Cook Political Report recently moved the contest from “likely Republican” to “lean Republican,” one notch from “toss-up.”

Marshall’s camp rejects the idea that Hamilton is a moderate. “Hamilton is a liberal Democrat who was just exposed for shaming his church for eating too much beef and preaching that Christians are dangerous — he won’t serve one term, let alone two,” Brent Robertson, Marshall’s chief of staff, said in a statement.

Hamilton defines himself as an “independent-minded Democrat” and has rebuffed national party leaders, including former Vice President Kamala Harris, who he has said would hurt his election chances if she showed up in Kansas to campaign for him.

“I think people in Kansas are looking for folks who are pretty much in the center,” Hamilton said. “There is a large segment of people who would consider themselves moderates — Republicans and Democrats. And the perceptions are that there are a lot of national Democrats who are further to the left than where people in Kansas are.”

“It’s a Republican state, it’s a red state,” he added. “I think people are willing to say, ‘I’ll consider voting for a Democrat, but I need to know that they align with my values, they line up with how I see the world,’ and that’s going to be people who are closer to the center.”

The crowd at a Hamilton event Friday night, held on a supporter’s front lawn in Eastborough, a Wichita suburb, spanned the political spectrum. Every voter who spoke to MS NOW cited the candidate’s centrist politics as a reason to back him.

“I think he’ll speak to all Kansans. He’s not there to just vote a party line,” said Dawn, 57, an independent who has voted for candidates from both parties, as a bluegrass band, Hamilton's warm-up act, strummed and sang at the foot of the front steps.

Dawn, who declined to give her last name, said she could not support a Republican “in the current atmosphere,” and that her husband, who declined an interview, “is a Republican who is frustrated with the Republican situation.”

A few feet away, Pam Harnden, a 77-year-old Republican, sat in a lawn chair. She said she was considering voting for Hamilton.

“I just like the fact that he’s thoughtful and is a good listener and I think would be more of a centrist position on things,” she said.

Hamilton, who leads the largest United Methodist church in the United States, benefits from an already high profile. Both Dawn and Harnden are Methodists and knew of him before he announced his Senate bid.

But his moderate message has also caught the attention of Cyndra Whiddon, a libertarian who said she was leaning toward voting for Hamilton as she waited in line for a cup of chili at a Wichita street fair.

Whiddon said she caught bits and pieces of Hamilton and Marshall's debate at the Kansas State Fair this month. “The only reason I really like him more than the other is at the beginning, he was very, like, ‘I’m middle of the road,’” she said.

“He’s not a politician,” she added. “He hasn’t been bought yet.”

news.title: James Talarico’s Texas Hype Train Has a 2024 Problem
news.text: The James Talarico hype train is thundering through Texas, powered by poll after poll showing the Democrat leads Republican rival Ken Paxton in a gripping Senate race that could flip a red state blue for the first time in, well, a long time. Talarico is young, charismatic, and devoutly Christian. He’s also liberal on issues like abortion and LGBTQ+ rights, once describing God as nonbinary, the kind of stance that has earned him the nickname "Tala-freak-o" among his Republican opponents. Paxton, on the other hand, is a classic, red-blooded Texas Republican, but one whose political career is checkered by scandal and controversy, including allegations of corruption. MAGA loves him; Texas isn’t so sure. It’s all looking like Talarico’s to lose right now. We’ve seen this story before. Remember Beto O’Rourke’s near-miss in 2018? But there’s a closer precedent that should slow the wheels of the Talarico train. And there’s a clear echo. One point. That’s Talarico’s lead over Paxton in Emerson College’s latest Texas poll, 47 percent to 46. It was also Ted Cruz’s lead over Colin Allred in Emerson’s final Texas poll of 2024, 48 to 47. Thirteen days later, Cruz won by 8.5 points. The polling echo isn’t a forecast. The candidates, the electorate, and the year are all different. But it is a warning about the story now being told in which Talarico’s leads are read as evidence that Texas is finally turning blue again. His edge in the major polling averages is three to four points. That’s smaller than the more than four-point miss Texas polls produced two years ago. And much of the likely-voter polling rests on assumptions about which 2024 voters will participate in a midterm. Which is this: the coalition that handed Donald Trump a nearly 14-point Texas win in 2024 will not fully turn out again. Underestimating Both Sides In 2024, the final polling averages had Cruz ahead by roughly four points, about half his eventual margin. Four years earlier, 2020, the incumbent Senator John Cornyn—defeated by Trump-endorsed Paxton in the GOP primary—went into Election Day about seven points up in the RealClearPolitics average and won by nearly 10. Both years, Trump was on the ballot. The midterms tell another story. In 2018, the final averages had Cruz ahead of O’Rourke by six to seven points. He won by 2.6, and Emerson’s own final poll, Cruz by three, was nearly exact. In 2022, the final University of Texas/Texas Politics Project poll had Greg Abbott up over O’Rourke by 11 in the gubernatorial race. He won by 10.9. The recent record does not flow in one direction. Texas polls understated the Democrat in 2018, came remarkably close in 2022, and understated the Republican Senate margin in both 2020 and 2024. They underestimated Republicans when Trump was on the ballot, and underestimated the Democrat in the last midterm fought under a President Trump. The Talarico Train Is Rolling None of this makes the Talarico train a mirage. Every nonpartisan survey in the Texas Politics Project’s tracker since late August has him ahead, by one to six points. His campaign had raised $68.6 million through June 30, against $9.2 million for Paxton’s committees—more at that stage than any Texas general-election candidate in a decade, with 51 percent from donors who have given less than $200. Paxton has the worst net favorability of any statewide candidate in Texas Southern University’s latest poll, 43 percent favorable to 55 unfavorable. And Republicans are acting as if the threat is urgent: conservative super PACs had spent $98.5 million on advertising by mid-September. What Pollsters Changed Pollsters rarely announce their changes, but their methodology notes, read side by side, show some were made. Emerson’s final 2024 Texas poll reached voters through automated landline calls, text messages, and a commercial online panel. This September’s poll contacted a probability-based voter panel by text, added interviews from a second panel, and matched panel responses to the voter file. Rice University’s Mark Jones co-led the University of Houston’s 2024 surveys, which relied on a YouGov online panel. The Texas Southern polls he now co-writes instead text a random sample of registered voters. The bet lives in the likely-voter screen. Texas Southern’s likely voters who cast 2024 ballots say they backed Trump 54 percent to 44—a 10-point margin, against his actual 13.7. Jones explained that, in a midterm, many of Trump’s 2024 supporters are "simply going to stay home this November" in Texas. The enthusiasm numbers support him in that assessment. In the Texas Politics Project’s August poll, 39 percent of Republicans said they were extremely enthusiastic about voting, down from 52 percent at the same point in 2022. It is also a bet on Hispanic voters, the group at the center of 2024’s surprise. Emerson’s September 2024 poll had them backing Kamala Harris 54 percent to 41, and Jones’s own Houston survey had them evenly split. Texas exit-poll estimates later suggested Trump won roughly 55 percent of Latino voters. But Emerson’s latest has them backing Talarico 54 to 39, a symptom, perhaps, of Trump’s aggressive immigration crackdown. Arriving at the Station The bet is reasonable—2018 is the precedent—but it’s going to be put to the test very soon. Paxton wins just 84 percent of Republicans in Texas Southern’s poll. Abbott, on the same ballot, wins 88. All else equal, merely closing the four-point gap between Paxton's and Abbott's support among Republicans would be arithmetically enough to erase Talarico's one-point lead. There are certainly hints they might. When Big Data Poll pushed undecided likely voters to choose, they broke toward Paxton, shrinking a three-point lead to two. When early voting opens October 19, watch out for whether turnout sags faster in Trump’s 2024 strongholds than in the Democratic cities. If it does, Talarico’s lead looks more plausible. Otherwise, the Emerson echo will stop sounding like a coincidence. Texas Democrats have waited three decades for this train, and Talarico has plainly got it moving. But a lead built on a turnout assumption is a timetable, not a destination—and Texas showed in 2024 what happens when the riders nobody counted suddenly turn up at the station looking for a different train.
news.summary: Will the Texas coalition that turned out for Donald Trump appear when the president is not on the ballot?

news.title: Fact Check: Did Trump Call Iowans 'Really Troubled People'?
news.text: A social media post reporting that President Donald Trump called Iowans “troubled people” during a White House announcement has gone viral. A user on X shared a clip of Trump from Monday's White House announcement of plans for a $15 billion mega-steel plant in Iowa to be built by Mesabi Metallics, which recently announced plans to invest $2.5 billion in building a new iron ore mine in Nashwauk, Minnesota. During the Oval Office press conference, Trump spoke with the president and chairman of the Export–Import Bank, John Jovanovic, about financing the Minnesota iron ore mine. This is when the “troubled people” comment was made. The Claim A progressive political X account, Headquarters (@HQNewsNow), shared a clip from Trump’s comments with the caption, “Trump claims the federal government can ‘supersede’ Iowa and calls Iowans ‘troubled people.’ ” The clip showed Trump checking whether the federal government could supersede a state government, saying “otherwise the state will…” before trailing off and adding, “They’re really troubled people.” The post on X had more than 421,000 views as of Tuesday, with some commenters pointing out that Trump was talking about Minnesota’s government, not Iowans. The Facts The “troubled people” comment was made during Trump’s exchange with Jovanovic. A full video of the event shows Jovanovic praising Trump for his plan and for contributing to “America’s economic security.” He then spoke about how the iron ore mine in Nashwauk is the first to have been opened in the United States in 50 years. He said Trump was helping “resurrect” the Iron Range (a region in the north of the state known for its iron ore deposits and mining communities), promising “one American supply chain…so we can assure that the war fighter of tomorrow is always well-equipped and that everyday Americans have what they need when they need it most.” Trump then asked how Democratic Minnesota Governor Tim Walz, a frequent adversary of the president, is treating the project, “because I freed up the iron ore…and then they closed it, and the people were devastated, because it is the finest iron ore in the world.” Trump went on to refer to Minnesota as “one of the worst-run places I’ve ever seen” and then remarked that the federal government can “supersede the state,” referring to the state’s Democratic leadership, adding, “They’re really troubled people.” It is not clear what law or state decision Trump thinks he may need to override—Newsweek has contacted the White House, via email, for comment. In 2021, Minnesota’s Department of Natural Resources terminated Mesabi Metallics’ state mineral leases, but this was over a lease dispute, according to court records. Mesabi Metallics has since secured its water and operational air permits, with Walz touring the site last August. “This project shows what’s possible when labor, industry, and communities come together to build for the future,” the governor said at the time. “Minnesota has a proud history as a leader in mining, with steelworkers who are second to none. We are excited to see this progress in Nashwauk.” The Context The social media post from HQNewsNow comes as Iowa has become a key midterm battleground. Even though Trump won the state by more than 9 percent in 2016 and by 13 percent in 2024 and the last time Democrats won an Iowa Senate election was 18 years ago, some recent polls show U.S. Senate candidate Josh Turek and gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand—both Democrats—have strong chances of winning their respective elections this November. Republican Representative Ashley Hinson, who Trump has endorsed in the race to replace retiring Republican Senator Joni Ernst, has broken with Trump on issues like the Iran war amid slipping approval numbers for the administration. Hinson has also called for the House to "return to D.C. immediately to work to pause diesel exports, suspend the gas tax, fully unleash E15 and biodiesel, and work on a diesel relief program for truckers and farmers." Trump’s steel announcement could help Hinson win over Republicans disillusioned with the administration and independents who “generally care less about the political stuff and care more about the ‘kitchen table’ issues,” as political science Professor Timothy M. Hagle, at the University of Iowa previously told Newsweek. The Ruling False. Trump was not calling Iowans “troubled people,” he was criticizing Minnesota’s Democratic leadership, specifically Walz, with whom he has long had tensions. This started during the 2024 election, when Walz ran as Kamala Harris’s vice-presidential nominee, but things escalated earlier this year, during Trump’s immigration operation in Minnesota, which Walz opposed. Newsweek has contacted Walz's office, via email, for comment.
news.summary: A progressive political account posted a snippet of Trump talking, saying he called Iowans "troubled people."

news.title: Trump gets bad news from the voters who helped deliver Florida
news.text:
President Donald Trump is seeing a weakening of support among certain Latino voters in Florida, a group that had helped him bolster the Republican coalition in 2024, as his administration's immigration enforcement moves further into the South Florida communities.

A Washington Post article states that Republican lawmakers in parts of Florida with a large Latino population are having to justify their support for Trump as they deal with voters who are dissatisfied with the way immigration enforcement is being managed. This tension is particularly apparent in Miami-Dade County, since Trump had won over Kamala Harris by more than 125,000 votes in 2024 following years of Republican support among Hispanic voters.

Rep. María Elvira Salazar of Florida, a member of the Republican Party, is one of the clearest examples of this. The representative, who covers a district that is about three-quarters Hispanic, put out a campaign advertisement this month explicitly asking Trump to alter his course.

Salazar told Trump in the advertisement that some of your immigration enforcement actions have gone too far. She also stated that Hispanic voters who had helped Trump get back to the White House now feel betrayed.

A poll conducted by the Republicans and provided to Axios at the beginning of this month showed the division among Hispanic voters in Miami-Dade. Sixty-three percent favoured the deportation of those immigrants who are in the country illegally, while 34 percent opposed it. However, when the question was asked about the way in which deportations were being carried out, only 29 percent approved and 58 percent disapproved.

The figures show that there is a difference between support for more rigorous immigration enforcement and dissatisfaction with certain tactics used by the administration.

The figures cited by The Post indicated that over half of those arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement in July had no criminal conviction and no outstanding criminal charges, while Reuters subsequently stated that more than three-quarters of the recent ICE arrests had concerned people who had no criminal convictions or charges.

Salazar is also having a harder reelection fight than the Republicans had originally anticipated. A poll carried out internally by Democratic candidate Eliott Rodriguez showed the two candidates tied at 45 percent, although internal campaign polling may not be reliable and the Cook Political Report still classifies the seat as "likely Republican".

Trump has dismissed Salazar's criticism. He had previously stated in this month that she had become "softer" on the border and maintained that his immigration policies were a major factor in his win in 2024.

Florida is still a firmly Republican state at the statewide level. In 2024, Trump received 56.1 percent of the vote, versus 43 per ent for Harris. However, the response in the heavily Latino part of South Florida gives Republicans a chance to see if the coalition that contributed to that margin will still be there by the 2026 midterms.

news.title: How I Got Dragged Into a Putin Disinformation Op
news.text:
A version of the below article first appeared in David Corn’s newsletter, Our Land. The newsletter comes out twice a week (most of the time) and provides behind-the-scenes stories and articles about politics, media, and culture. Subscribing costs just $5 a month—but you can sign up for a free 30-day trial.

I just published a book that exposes Russian disinformation operations. Now I—that is, a fake version of me—have become part of a Russian disinformation operation.

How Russia Won: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin, and the Fight for America chronicles the shadow war of clandestine influence and disinformation operations—many implemented to aid Trump—that Putin has been mounting against the United States for a decade. It ends with the warning that Moscow would likely attack the ongoing midterm elections to help Trump and the GOP. Within days of the book’s publication two weeks ago, media outlets reported that Russia’s disinformation operatives, using phony accounts on social media platforms, had started hurling derogatory material at Democrats.

Last week, this covert disinformation operation widened to spread scurrilous allegations against Democratic candidates—phony accusations that were falsely attributed to me.

So after writing a book about Putin’s disinformation efforts and noting they posed a threat to the current elections, I am being used by a Russian disinformation network to influence the midterms in Trump’s favor. This is a bizarre snake-eating-its-tail situation.

In the book, I report on several secret Russian disinformation units that produced and disseminated false allegations about Vice President Kamala Harris and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz during the 2024 campaign. One was dubbed Matryoshka by disinformation trackers. (That’s the name for those iconic Russian nesting dolls.) It zapped out on X and other social media platforms assorted lies about Harris: She had an abortion when she was 17. She was exhibiting early-onset Alzheimer’s. Her grandfather was a communist. Her family was connected to Pfizer and Big Pharma.

When news organizations recently revealed that Matryoshka was at it again, this time concocting videos that purported to be CNN news segments covering Hollywood celebrities trash-talking Democrats (Nazi whores!), I reported that these covert operatives were also generating and posting fake videos that appeared to be CNN spots with damaging information on Democratic senatorial candidates. James Talarico (Texas) “despises” Hasidic Jews because they don’t allow gender affirmation treatment. Sherrod Brown (Ohio) owns a business that has “caused the bee population in Ohio to decline by a factor of nine.” Jon Ossoff (Georgia) has “called for a complete halt to military aid to Israel and for all resources to be redirected to Ukraine.” And there were others.

While I was working on that story, @antibot4navalny, a group of anonymous activists who monitor Russian disinformation, informed me that Matryoshka had also posted on X a supposed Mother Jones video that reported that the Democratic Party had paid $289 million to Mark Thompson, the head of CNN, so the cable news network would run reports that “promote gender transition among minors.” I quickly published a piece exposing this absurd disinformation. After a lawyer for Mother Jones contacted X, the company took down this fraudulent video.

But Matryoshka was not done with Mother Jones—or me.

On Friday, @antibot4navalny informed me that Matryoshka—through an obvious bot account on X—had posted a purported CNN video of me promoting a new book. But the book isn’t How Russia Won. It’s supposedly called Enemies of Democracy for Dummies, and the video declared, “The book will feature over 300 stories related to crimes committed by members of the Democratic Party.”

This counterfeit video displayed the text of a made-up quote from me: “Apparently, there’s a fissure somewhere in the US that leads straight to hell; otherwise, I don’t understand where all these devils from the Democratic Party are coming from.” That’s quite the analysis. The video noted that “information from David Corn’s book will further damage the Democrats’ reputation and standing ahead of the elections.”

Here are screenshots from that video:

To be clear, none of this is true—though Enemies of Democracy for Dummies is not a bad idea for a book.

Again, a lawyer for Mother Jones reached out to X. But by then, it was the weekend, and this fake CNN video claiming I had published a book full of dirt on Democrats that would affect the election remained online. It looked as if it initially drew nearly 200,000 views, but I was reliably informed that Matryoshka was using bots to juice this number and that this post likely had only reached a few thousand X users.

As with the previous fake and nonsensical video reporting that Mother Jones had revealed a $289 million payment from the DNC to CNN’s chief for pro-trans coverage, this one seemed a bit too silly to have much impact. It was more of an irritation than a cause of great concern.

Then came other fake videos.

Matryoshka, using old bot accounts created up to 12 years ago, spewed out at least nine sham Mother Jones videos, with each one promoting an outrageous but spurious allegation about a Democratic candidate. One “revealed” that a Democratic senatorial candidate “is a closeted gay man who hides his sexual orientation in order to maintain a luxurious lifestyle.” It said he had previously been accused of “embezzling public funds to pay for the services of male sex workers.”

With ominous synth music playing, this video segues to footage of me and written text in which I purportedly state that in my Enemies of Democracy for Dummies book “I present evidence” this Democratic candidate “dated underaged boys and had sexual relations with them.” The quote continues: “As a gay man, I find it outrageous that a gay man would hide behind a woman to maintain his lavish lifestyle.” (Not that it matters, but I’m not gay.) The video ends with a card saying, “Read more at MotherJones.com.”

Throughout this one-and-a-half-minute video, the Mother Jones logo appears in the top right corner.

The other videos are all in the same style. (For obvious reasons, I am not linking to them or mentioning the candidates by name.) They claim that a Democratic candidate for governor who served in Vietnam “is suspected of killing 37 civilians” in a massacre during that war, that another Democratic gubernatorial candidate recruited minors into sex work and “while working for the Girl Scouts…organized sex parties for members of the Democratic Party,” that a third Democratic candidate for governor caused “a fatal car accident while under the influence of alcohol,” and that another Democratic gubernatorial nominee sold crack to college students, “resulting in 17 deaths,” and so on.

Each of these videos features me offering a colorful quote about the allegation and noting it’s straight out of Enemies of Democracy for Dummies. Similar to the bogus video about the DNC payment to the CNN chief, some of these X posts show nearly 200,000 views. But the real numbers are likely much lower. They have not, as of this writing, gone viral. (X did not respond immediately to a request to delete the posts with these videos.)

So the journalist who wrote a book to call attention to Putin’s disinformation crusade against American democracy is now being used by Moscow’s disinformation operatives to subvert the midterm elections for Trump’s benefit.

I’ve been asked by colleagues and friends if this is frightening. Not yet. Perhaps these phony videos are meant to be a brushback pitch. Mostly, it’s unnerving—a demonstration of how easy it is to be misrepresented and exploited by unidentified scoundrels. And, as we all know, it’s tough to beat back a lie on the internet. We’re all vulnerable to a cyber assault.

There are five weeks to go to Election Day. How extensive might Putin’s war on the midterms become? How far will he go to boost Trump and the Republicans? If Trump tries to spark chaos and a crisis with accusations of vote fraud or actions to interfere with the election and the vote tally, Putin’s disinformation army can be expected to do whatever it can to bolster any false claims and conspiracy theories flying about—or to cook up its own.

One reason I wrote How Russia Won was to counter the false “Russia, Russia, Russia” narrative peddled relentlessly for years by Trump, Republicans, MAGA influencers, and right-wing media personalities who have denied Russia has been covertly intervening in US elections. By echoing Putin’s own denials, these useful idiots have been complicit in a foreign adversary’s attack on American democracy. My point was to show the United States has been under continuous assault from Moscow, as Russia has schemed to assist Trump and the Republicans. With this disinformation operation incorporating truly fake news about me, Putin’s Matryoshka crew has proved the premise of my book.

news.title: Rivals for LA mayor set to meet in forum as city struggles with homelessness, Hollywood job losses
news.text:
LOS ANGELES (AP) — Two Democratic rivals seeking to lead troubled Los Angeles will meet in a high-stakes forum Tuesday just days before mail ballots drop, as voters weigh whether to stick with unpopular incumbent Karen Bass or turn to a little-known City Council member backed by the Democratic Socialists of America, Nithya Raman.

The contest has raised the possibility that the nation’s second most populous city could follow New York’s lead, where democratic socialist Zohran Mamdani was elected mayor, capping a stunning ascent for the far-left state lawmaker who promised to transform city government to restore power to the working class. Yet in LA, no celebrity swirl has gathered around Raman in her first run for citywide office.

The two Democrats are scheduled to appear at a forum sponsored by the Jewish Federation Los Angeles at a time when the party has been deeply divided over the war in Gaza and aid to Israel.

Bass, the first Black woman to hold the post, is fighting to keep her job after a rough first term in which she suffered sustained fallout from the deadly Palisades Fire, the most destructive in Los Angeles history that ignited when she was out of the country. In June, a fire east of downtown in a massive frozen-food warehouse left neighbors to endure weeks of foul smells and frustration.

Raman, who endorsed Bass before reversing course and entering the race herself, is testing if voters in the heavily Democratic city want to move further to the political left to address long-running problems of homelessness, buckled streets and climbing rent and home prices. She’s railed against “the broken status quo.”

The race earlier garnered national attention for the candidacy of Spencer Pratt, a Republican who starred on “The Hills” and had lost his home in the Palisades Fire. His campaign was lifted by videos that supporters generated with artificial intelligence, though he failed to qualify for the November election.

In a city known to shrug at local politics, the race to take charge at City Hall has been overshadowed by ongoing turmoil in Washington, the fight for Congress, two wars, anxiety over inflation and the Los Angeles Dodgers gearing up for another playoff run.

On the horizon are questions about how the financially challenged city will manage the 2028 Olympics.

After the fires, “There are a bunch of people who don’t want to vote for Karen (Bass) and they are wrestling with what to do,” said veteran Democratic strategist Bill Carrick. As a council member, Raman is not widely known and “the decibel level of this campaign is unbelievably low.”

With mail ballots scheduled to arrive at homes in early October, typical markers of election season — yard signs, TV ads, billboards and bumper stickers — are rarely seen. Data compiled by AdImpact shows the campaigns have spent or booked only a sprinkle of airtime and digital messaging so far through Election Day.

Bass took office in 2022 promising to contend with an out-of-control homeless crisis, but the problem remains in plain view in most neighborhoods. Figures released in July showed homelessness increased over the previous year, after taking a dip. Bass faulted the Trump administration for cuts and policies “that pushed more people onto the streets.”

During her time in office, the city has weathered federal immigration raids and witnessed a continuing exit of Hollywood jobs, while residents complain about dirty, crumbling streets and homeless encampments.

Raman, who could be the first South Asian woman in the job, says while City Hall has favored powerful insiders “working people pay the price in higher rents, depleted services and a city that has stopped working for them.”

Bass represents the Democratic establishment as the incumbent mayor, and she’s backed by Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, along with influential labor unions. She served in the state Legislature and Congress before becoming mayor in 2022.

Raman has promised to speed up housing construction, bring back entertainment industry jobs and improve services in a city known for filthy streets, gridlock and an unresponsive City Hall.

One of the unknowns in the race is where Pratt’s supporters will go, if they vote at all. Pratt finished with about 25% of the vote, several points behind Raman. He’s continued to criticize both candidates on social media.

“Truly the Dumb and Dumber election. So sad for LA. Dark times ahead, folks,” he recently posted on X.

news.title: Will Trump's Ohio Visit Rescue Jon Husted? What Polling Data Shows
news.text: President Donald Trump is heading to Ohio on Saturday to campaign for Jon Husted, as the Ohio senator staves off a challenge from former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown. Brown has mounted a competitive campaign. Recent polls have generally shown Brown with narrow leads over Husted, according to poll aggregator RealClearPolling, which has marked the race a toss-up. The Democrat's advantage is particularly pronounced among younger voters. A recent poll from Quantus Insights, conducted September 21-23, found Brown leading Husted 51 percent to 31 percent among voters aged 18 to 29, and 50 percent to 39 percent among those aged 30 to 44. Meanwhile, the Republican led among older voters. This poll surveyed 695 likely voters and has a 4.2 percent margin of error. A spokesperson for Husted’s campaign told Newsweek in an emailed statement that they do not comment on public polling, but said: "We are looking forward to welcoming President Trump to Ohio, a state he won decisively three times." Newsweek contacted Brown’s campaign for comment on Monday and is awaiting a response. Trump's Ohio Strength Faces Test Among Younger Voters Trump is making the visit to Vandalia, Ohio, this weekend as part of a broader effort to campaign for Republicans in competitive races ahead of the November midterms. Trump won Ohio in all three elections he ran in, and remains an important Republican figure in the state. However, his approval among younger Americans in Ohio has deteriorated, raising questions about how much his popularity translates to the voters among whom Husted is trailing. A Civiqs poll found that 70 percent of 18- to 34-year-olds in Ohio disapprove of how the president is handling his job, as do 62 percent of 35- to 49-year-olds. Ballots don't record voters' ages, so it is difficult to ascertain Trump’s performance among younger voters in Ohio in the 2024 election. Exit poll research by Edison Research suggested that Trump narrowly won voters aged 18 to 29 in Ohio in 2024 by three percentage points, but lost voters aged 30 to 44 to Kamala Harris by one percentage point. Other exit poll estimates differ. Fox News’ exit poll research in 2024 found Trump leading Harris across all age groups in the state. The latest polling raises questions about how much Trump can help Husted close the gap with Brown among younger voters. Sherrod’s Challenge Brown is seeking a comeback two years after losing his Senate seat to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024. A longtime Ohio politician, Brown had held the seat since 2007, even as Ohio moved increasingly Republican, until his recent loss. Husted, a longtime Ohio politician who has held several elected state positions, took up Ohio’s other Senate seat in January 2025 after it was vacated by JD Vance when he became vice president. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Matthew Cannon and James Debens
news.summary: Donald Trump is heading to Ohio as Jon Husted trails Sherrod Brown in recent Senate race polls.

news.title: Trump Busted Hiding Embarrassing Reality in Late-Night Brag
news.text:
Donald Trump has shared a tiny portion of a CNN video that defended the president while conveniently removing the rest, which savaged his dire polling numbers.

In a late-night Truth Social post, the 80-year-old shared a 43-second clip of Harry Enten, CNN’s chief data analyst, showing how Trump’s MAGA base is sticking with the president.

However, the full Enten segment, released online Monday, is more than 14 minutes long and reveals multiple examples of non-MAGA Republicans and GOP lawmakers deserting the president ahead of the Nov. 3 midterms.

This includes Enten revealing an “eye-popping” stat at the start of the video that less than 1 percent of GOP political ads that aired in the first half of September mentioned Trump, compared with 20 percent of Democratic ads.

“So, is this finally a sign that the Republican base is abandoning Donald Trump?” Enten asked about the president, whose near record-low approval ratings could doom the GOP in November.

“When it comes to non-MAGA, this is where we’ve absolutely seen Donald Trump’s numbers plummet into the ocean,” Enten said.

Enten noted that in the 2024 election, non-MAGA Republicans favored Trump over Kamala Harris by 56 points. However, Trump’s approval rating among this demographic has now plummeted to just seven points during his turbulent second term.

“That is a shift, my dear friends, of 49 points away from the president of the United States among non-MAGA Republicans,” Enten said. “So his support is definitely not just ebbing there, but is absolutely crashing there.”

Enten also showed that just 46 percent of non-MAGA Republicans are “extremely motivated” to vote in the midterms, compared with 71 percent of Democratic voters, which could have dire implications for the GOP.

Later in the segment, Enten revealed that around 10 percent of non-MAGA Republicans said they will vote for a Democratic candidate in November, and that Trump’s approval rating among the key independent demographic has plunged 86 percentage points to minus 71 compared with the 2024 election.

“The same thing that is bringing Trump’s approval rating down with Republican voters is what’s impacting him among independent voters: It’s the economy,” Enten said. “In the fall of 2024, Donald Trump, among pure independents, was trusted more to handle the economy than Kamala Harris by a 22-point margin. His net approval rating now is minus 77 points.”

He added: “When it comes to the wallet … what’s really hurting Donald Trump? Well, it’s the gas prices.” 

The video also revealed that 92 percent of independent voters disapprove of Trump’s handling of gas prices, which have soared during the war with Iran.

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.
