news.title: The Patriot Post® · What Did Racial Gerrymandering Really Accomplish?
news.text:
There are 535 members of Congress. Representatives chosen by qualified Americans fill those seats, in a system defined by political equality and economic liberty. 

The U.S. Supreme Court inverted this principle in 1986 with the Thornburg v Gingles decision. Attempting to equalize economic outcomes, political power was unequally allocated to congressional districts drawn with a majority of black voters. This scheme aimed to right the effects of historic wrongs and drew broad support from citizens across the country. 

Embedded in the decision was the racist idea that all blacks think the same, an affront to American principles. In this pre-DEI, misguided mindset, Nature’s God in our Declaration of Independence allocates sovereignty by skin color. There is no colorblind individuality our government must humble itself before, just tribes of belief.

SCOTUS reversed that disgraceful policy in April with Louisiana v Callais, ending an era in which states were humiliatingly scrutinized — Southern states, that is — on their conformity to court-ordered racial quotas in congressional mapping. The fact that every such “majority-minority” congressional seat went to a Democrat in a Republican state, with an ever-expanding number of such districts, was presumed to be justice at work.

Democrat civil rights and congressional leaders such as Kamala Harris, Chuck Schumer, Hakeem Jeffries, and Al Sharpton have decried the Callais ruling as a return to “Jim Crow” and an attack on voting rights. Broadly speaking, they infer it is a political effort to achieve white nationalism.

A new report from RealAmerica.Vote challenges this claim. Researchers investigated outcomes for six majority-minority districts formed or protected by the early 1990s under the Voting Rights Act Section 2. Given the immense opportunity for political, educational and economic transformation generously apportioned by the American people, what transpired? Did the opportunity for black racial blocs to choose congressional representation equalize socioeconomic conditions in those districts as compared to surrounding districts?

Six districts (AL-7, GA-5, LA-2, MS-2, SC-6, VA-3) were selected for study since they persisted throughout the duration (2000–2024) without being overturned or invalidated by the court and maintained a majority or at least a plurality of black voters throughout. 

A set of “Basic” (e.g., employment) and aspirational “American Dream” needs (e.g., own a home) were used to measure the socioeconomic performance of these districts. Data were sourced from the Census for 2000 and the American Community Survey. 

The districts have seen, at best, only a slight improvement in meeting basic and aspirational needs of majority-minority black districts. Recent boundary changes in GA-5 and LA-2 appear to be driving a lot of the observed improvement, so it is hard to say whether single-member minority congressional representation improved the situation at all. 

Analysis resulted in examples like the chart below, where the prevalence of single motherhood ranged from 39-46% worse in majority-minority districts than surrounding districts, for 24 years. Blacks who were stuck stayed stuck. 

The data shows that Democrats locked in control of densely black-populated swaths of the South for decades, failed the incredible leadership opportunity to uplift them, and used national taxpayer dollars to incentivize broken homes and government dependence over rebuilding stable families and developing economic and individual civic potential. All six majority-minority black districts studied significantly lag their peer state districts across all need areas.

With the return of colorblind political representation, we have a new opportunity. Using the great principles of our founding including limited government, political equality, rule of law, free markets, education in American civics to build engaged citizens, and incentives to hard work such as low taxes and respect for property rights we can engage the potential of every American who develops their God-given gifts within the framework of our social contract. 

Will Callais will be the Economic Emancipation Proclamation for America’s marginalized black populations? The answer depends on each of us voting for representatives who boldly support and defend our core national values of political equality and economic liberty, known to Americans as the right to pursue happiness.

news.title: Mike Rogers can win this U.S. Senate race: Here's how
news.text:
The storyline that has emerged in the last couple of weeks of national polling and in Michigan's closely watched U.S. Senate race is that, with Democrats ascendant, Republican nominee Mike Rogers' chances of beating Abdul El-Sayed are declining, perhaps precipitously.

As with any story worth telling, though, there can always be a surprise.

Rogers, a former GOP congressman from White Lake, has cause for concern, trailing by 3 percentage points in the RealClearPolling.com average of polls with five weeks to go until the Nov. 3 election and most of the recent polls showing El-Sayed extending his lead.

And the headwinds he and other Republicans face are clear enough: Inflation remains high. Gasoline and diesel prices are up significantly due to an unpopular war started by President Donald Trump, whose own popularity is at or near record lows. National generic ballot polls, which ask those surveyed which party they would support in Congress if the election were held now, have shown Democratic support ahead and growing.

Then there's the historical trends — the party in power, right now the Republicans, tends to lose seats in midterm elections. Michigan's not friendly ground to Republican U.S. Senate candidates anyway, having not elected one since Spencer Abraham in 1994, which was a wave year for the GOP.

But it's not a fait accompli. In Michigan at this point in the presidential race in 2016, Hillary Clinton was favored in the polling average to beat Donald Trump by 5 points and no Republican presidential nominee had won the state since George H.W. Bush in 1988. Trump won it in 2016 by two-tenths of a percentage point, shocking most observers, but not all.

"I think Michigan is competitive and will be until Election Day," said U.S. Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Ann Arbor, who warned that Michigan was still very much in play in 2016. "I'd rather be in our position than in their position (this year).

"But Republicans are going to pour a ton of money into this race… Everyone needs to know their votes matter."

Rogers has a few things going for him that could help him win this race, which remains perhaps the GOP's best chance in the nation to flip a Democratic seat in the Senate and keep that party from potentially regaining a majority.

Two years ago, he came within a hair's breadth — or in that case, 19,006 votes, or three-tenths of a percentage point — of winning a Senate seat, losing to then-U.S. Rep. Elissa Slotkin, but also giving his campaign confidence it could do even better this time.

"Last cycle, we got more votes than any statewide Republican (Senate) candidate in Michigan history. Now, it’s just a matter of turning those voters out," Rogers told the Free Press.

But it's not just that he ran an inarguably strong effort in 2024 that could lift Rogers and change the storyline, this time. Here's a rundown of what some of those factors and opportunities are or might be.

The polls could be wrong (aka will younger voters turn out?)

This is a gimme, but it's legitimate. And we don't need to look as far back as 2016 to give it some credence. In 2024, in Michigan, the polling average in the presidential race had Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris slightly ahead of Trump, who was trying to reclaim the White House after losing to Joe Biden in 2020. Trump won by 1.5 points. (And that's not a polling error, given that most polls have a margin of error of plus or minus 3-5 percentage points.)

Perhaps more significantly, in the Aug. 4 Democratic primary, the polling average had El-Sayed ahead of U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens of Birmingham by 10 percentage points. He ended up winning by 1.

Rogers joked with the Free Press in a recent interview that polling has gotten to be so disconnected to the results that his new rule is: "If I'm winning, I believe it."

But there is a real concern about the accuracy of Michigan polls in this race regarding the makeup of the electorate, specifically as to how many younger voters — who tend to be more supportive of El-Sayed — are represented in surveys compared to previous election results, and compared to older voters.

A recent poll by Suffolk University in Boston had El-Sayed ahead of Rogers 47%-40%, the largest margin in the race anyone has projected to date. That poll, however, had 23% of those surveyed age 18-34, when that bloc hasn't reached 19% in any midterm election in Michigan in the last 20 years, per data provided by Mark Grebner at Practical Political Data in Lansing and crunched by the Free Press. That poll also appeared to underestimate the participation of voters age 65 and up, which hasn't fallen below 30% in the last three midterms (and with whom Rogers tends to do better, if not win outright).

"I think that the older voters are definitely going to be the heavier influence in this election, no doubt in my mind," said Rogers, who, having not faced a competitive primary instead spent months knocking on doors and marching in parades up and down the state, hoping to add to what was already a more visible profile after his narrow loss to Slotkin two years ago. "They're gambling that they're going to have a (huge) turnout of the youth vote."

The case for the standard-issue senator with money to burn

Rogers is a staunchly conservative Republican, opposed to abortion rights, pro-business, and has a history of supporting American military intervention abroad. And he and his allies have been trying to make the case, through copious campaign appearances and political ads that he's the safer choice, claiming that El-Sayed is too close to the nation's enemies, sympathetic to terrorists, supportive of socialist policies, willing to defund the police; that El-Sayed is untested, unknown.

"His rhetoric is dangerous," Rogers said. "He's just way too extreme."

Much of this has been unpacked before: El-Sayed himself is unquestionably a progressive firebrand Democrat in the mold of Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont; having called for the elimination of Immigration and Custom Enforcement (with its core tasks being transferred to other agencies); supporting a single government-run health insurance plan for all Americans (meaning universal access, though other people would lose the insurance they currently have and raising questions about how it would be paid for); having questioned funding for police (though he has rescinded much of that position); and opposing military intervention in the Middle East, unrestricted funding for Israel and corporate hegemony over U.S. policy. (He rejects the socialist tag, saying he's a capitalist, but also a realist.)

El-Sayed has been a harsh critic of the Netanyahu government's practices in Israel and campaigned with Hasan Piker, an Internet influencer who himself has made controversial remarks he has since rescinded about U.S. policy leading to the 9/11 attacks (and which El-Sayed called "dumb"), as well as criticisms of Israel that some considered antisemitic (a characterization Piker denies). Some of El-Sayed's family members have voiced sympathy to the effects of Israeli counterattacks against Hamas in Gaza, though claims leveled at him for it by Trump were misleading, lacked context or were wrong. And El-Sayed himself has denounced all political violence, military spending abroad (except in cases like that of Ukraine) and antisemitism and Islamophobia.

El-Sayed is electric, but he is not your standard-issue U.S. senator from Michigan, a group that has tended to come across as more of a mold: no-nonsense legislators, strong campaigners, passable speakers, behind-the-scenes operatives, their expertise and contacts culled in the lower chamber.

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County and Detroit health director, has never been elected to public office. Rogers, on the other hand, has most of those qualifications, though he hasn't served in the House since his 2001-2015 stint, when he became chairman of the House Select Committee on Intelligence.

Rogers also was an FBI agent and served in the state Senate. El-Sayed and Democrats can and do chide Rogers for his ties to businesses, his support for pharmaceutical companies and his having lived in Florida. But Rogers can legitimately claim he helped pass prescription drug coverage for Medicare recipients (though he voted against letting it negotiate drug prices) and helped create Michigan's higher education savings plan.

Democrats have largely coalesced around El-Sayed (who already had the UAW in his corner) in recent weeks. But Rogers can also point to support from law enforcement and business groups, including the Michigan Chamber of Commerce and the Detroit Regional Chamber, which routinely endorses Democrats and notably did not endorse either Rogers or Slotkin two years ago.

In a state as connected to manufacturing as Michigan is, those endorsements could matter.

Appealing to Jewish Democrats, Black voters and others

So could be the question of where Jewish Democrats land. Some have made clear they'll bolt to Rogers; others continue to urge El-Sayed to voice support for Jewish self-determination in Israel while leaving their political preference in doubt. Others are backing El-Sayed, some as a partisan political issue.

A report from Brandeis University five years ago, estimated there were about 105,000 Jewish adults in Michigan, about 60% of whom identified as Democrats. Harvey Bronstein, a retired Oakland Community College professor active in Democratic politics and in the Jewish community, guessed as many as half of Jewish Democrats might vote for Rogers.

According to Rogers' campaign, he's engaging in significant outreach with Jewish Democrats, Blacks (who split over El-Sayed's candidacy in the primary) and other constituencies that may lean more Democratic in most years, but who he says are doubtful about supporting El-Sayed.

"Abdul is really extreme," Rogers said. "I've had opportunities now to get into these communities, to have conversations in these communities I never would have had except for Abdul's extreme positions, his rhetoric... That's been a huge opportunity for us."

Then — though Rogers didn't specifically mention this as an advantage — there's El-Sayed's name, his Muslim faith and his Egyptian heritage (he was born in Michigan). As the Free Press has reported, bias is a factor in this and other political races.

Put that together with the funding advantage Rogers and his allies appear to have — Rogers trailed El-Sayed in terms of overall fundraising as of the middle of July but had twice as much cash on hand at the time and Republican-aligned groups were set to spend another $49 million on the race compared to about half that for Democrats as of this week — and it gives Rogers something to work with.

Though that El-Sayed is too extreme argument cuts both ways.

There has been a noted shift away from the standard-issue politicians of the past in both parties, where partisan convention has been traded for unorthodox positioning and rhetorical bombast: El-Sayed began his primary campaign asking, "Where is the fight?" And just look at Trump's success.

And Andrea Bitely, founder and principal of Bitely Communications in Lansing who worked previously for former Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan on his independent gubernatorial run and for Republican former state Attorney General Bill Schuette, thinks the negative tone is "getting to the point where it’s starting to look desperate on the part of the Rogers campaign."

"It's their only play" though, she acknowledged.

“We’re pitching a big tent that welcomes Michiganders of all backgrounds and walks of life," said Rogers. "Democrats for Mike Rogers has been such a huge success, we had to order new yard signs! Michiganders are worried about how extreme Abdul is ... They know that we’re focused on solutions, not just slogans.”

Distancing himself from President Trump

Rogers owes this second bite at the political apple in Michigan to Trump, who endorsed Rogers in 2024 against Slotkin and again in this year's race. The moves were a bit of a surprise to some politicos given that Rogers, a regular contributor on CNN, criticized Trump's efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election.

Since then, however, Rogers has defended pretty much every suggestion Trump has made, from tariffs that as a free-trading Michigan congressman seemed incongruous to his previous positions, to delaying the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge (though he was among the first to announce the deal to open the bridge was reached and never cast doubt on its eventual opening). And he defended Trump's war with Iran.

"Michigan families are struggling with the price of everyday life," Rogers said in an ad on Sept. 21, as El-Sayed was preparing to welcome former Vice President (and former Democratic presidential nominee) Kamala Harris into Detroit to campaign with him. "Groceries cost too much. We have to bring prices down. The war with Iran needs to end and end quickly."

It was a refrain taken up by Republican candidates around the Midwest and one El-Sayed and Democrats characterized as a disingenuous flip-flop, an 11th hour attempt to save themselves, especially as El-Sayed hammers Rogers on the campaign trail over the war and its effect on prices.

To be sure, Trump has shown no inclination to scale back the war or his rhetoric. And maybe the effort by Rogers is too little, too late; voters aren't likely to let anyone off the hook for gas and diesel prices until they start to come down significantly, if then. But splitting with an unpopular president might be worth a try: just ask former Vice President Harris after her failed 2024 presidential run.

Problem is, as with Harris, it's hard to go back on positions you've already supported, especially in recent memory, and get voters to believe you. Rogers, when speaking to the Free Press, made clear that he has never been and would never be for any trade policy that hurts Michigan, but believes Trump's import levies have improved conditions for manufacturing in the state. (He points to General Motors moving some production from Mexico back into the U.S., including to Orion Assembly in Michigan, as an example.)

It also sounds as though the plan is to argue that El-Sayed supports the same Democratic initiatives that led to inflation when Biden was president (though, in fact much of that inflation was a worldwide trend after the COVID-19 shutdowns and was declining before Biden left office).

"All of the things Republicans have been doing are trying to get those prices down permanently," Rogers said.

That seems to include the war.

"The president came in, he did a lot of deregulation. He did a lot of increase in American energy (production). We've got to make sure that we are less sensitive to world events by producing American energy," Rogers said. "We haven't gotten there yet."

He said he wasn't ready, at least at this point, to offer any other break with the president. But he says the state needs someone who can walk into the Oval Office and say, "Mr. President, this isn't working for Michigan."

Rogers has a little over five weeks until the election, but less than that to change the prevailing narrative. Debates set for Oct. 8 and Oct. 21 could help, though it would help his cause if the mood and the polls begin to swing within a week or two.

Still, it's unlikely that El-Sayed will win by the 7 points he predicted last spring. Right now, Rogers is behind by about the margin of error of most polls. The percentage of voters of both parties who vote straight-ticket ballots has been up in recent years, but if that were to shift for whatever reason it could provide another opportunity for Rogers; the same is true if Blacks in Detroit don't show up as strongly as they might for El-Sayed, as happened in the primary, when Stevens beat him nearly 2-to-1, and his efforts to court that vote since fall flat. And then there's that youth vote and whether it materializes.

Of course, Rogers also has to contend with his own realities, the possibility of a disenchanted Republican base and lower-frequency conservative voters staying home because Trump isn't on the ballot.

Rogers insists his ground game is top notch, that his people have knocked on millions of doors and he's seeing unrivaled enthusiasm for him in this race — and in places where he hasn't seen it before. He expects it will show up in the final result, that the stakes are too great for it not to.

"All the fancy TikTok dancing and well-scripted, well-choreographed events (by El-Sayed), all of that, that's great," said Rogers. "But I tell you what, we've invested in the last year and a half where people weren't paying attention and talking to real people."

"We’re talking about how we’re running to fix everything that’s broken in this state, from getting kids reading at grade level again, to investing in skilled trades, and making life more affordable," he added. "The contrast is clear. We’re confident Michiganders will choose right this November.”

news.title: Trump Used to Be Good at Attacking the Press. Things Have Changed.
news.text:
Donald Trump’s war on the press usually comes from a place of strength. After all, not only has Trump traditionally been a ratings magnet, but he’s also the president of the United States. That’s a position that tends to give you pretty good leverage.

In his second term, he has consistently picked when he has had the advantage. In his legally dubious lawsuits against CBS over the network editing an interview of Kamala Harris, he had the leverage of the company’s pending merger with Skydance—a merger which required approval from a top Trump ally on the Federal Communications Commission. It was the same when he tried to ban the Associated Press from the White House unless they adopted his preferred nomenclature of “Gulf of America” for the Gulf of Mexico. Either the company that writes the definitive stylebook for the American media would bend to his will or it would weaken the nonprofit press syndicate by making it far more difficult to provide White House coverage at a time when print journalism is facing increased financial pressure.

That’s not the case with the latest offensive he’s launched in a war with the media that started long before his entry into presidential politics and dates back to various feuds with local reporters when Trump was simply a New York real estate investor.

His effort to expel CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House does not come from a place of leverage. Instead, it happened impulsively, at a time when Trump’s political fortunes are at a nadir. His favorability rating in polling is even lower than it was in the immediate aftermath of the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol and when polling suggests Republicans are poised to lose at least one chamber of Congress in the coming midterms. Trump has always had an outsize interest in the media and certain savvy in maximizing his coverage. After all, the former host of Celebrity Apprentice has long had an abiding appreciation of what camera angles are best to capture him and a taste for even relatively obscure media gossip. But this maneuver feels more like a desperate gesture to try to do something to refocus the public’s attention as Trump sinks lower in opinion polls than a calculated effort to change the narrative.

Trump’s lashing out at the networks was reportedly prompted by his aide Natalie Harp, who, as Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan report in their book Regime Change, serves as a human binkie for Trump. On a Friday afternoon, while senior White House staffers were off campus, she showed Trump snippets of coverage that led to his sudden decision to ban the three outlets from the White House.

The three outlets quickly won a legal order from a federal judge to be allowed back into the White House. After being forced to let offending media outlets back in, Trump then tried to block CNN’s ability to participate in the White House Television Pool, a group that also includes NBC, CBS, ABC, and Fox News, in which each network alternates turns in the small group of reporters that travels with the president and is granted access to all public events.

Since Trump’s decision to ban CNN, the other television networks had refused to provide pool coverage of Trump in solidarity. The White House has been inconsistent about giving access to CNN in recent days since a federal judge ordered the administration to allow CNN back on White House grounds. However, they blocked CNN from covering Trump’s trip to a football game in Tennessee on Saturday. Other networks refused to fill in. However, the networks, according to the New York Times, have decided everything is too important to leave the president without any up-close television coverage indefinitely. The Associated Press’ litigation over being banned from the White House pool has gone on for nearly a year and a half without a resolution.

In other words, Trump has gone through an epic feud with the media over the past 10 days simply to ensure that he does not face questions from CNN, at least in the short term, in situations where only pool reporters are available to ask him questions. After all, while CNN’s reporters may not be allowed in the Oval Office, he’ll still face questions from CBS, ABC, and NBC (not to mention Fox, which is justifiably wary of a precedent that could allow, say, President Ocasio-Cortez to enact a similar ban on them).

The costs, though, have been high. At a time when the conflict with Iran is stalemated and gas prices keep on rising, it did not convey to voters that Trump had his priorities in order when he seemed far more focused on besting Kaitlan Collins than on Khamenei. It also meant that Trump’s much-vaunted state visit from Chinese strongman Xi Jinping went uncovered while other networks were refusing to participate in the television pool. Certainly, the attempts from niche right-wing streamers (let alone the White House’s own Trump TV) have not proved to be effective substitutes. (After all, even C-SPAN relies on the television when they broadcast events live.) Even those moments that were covered, such as Trump’s unveiling of the new White House helicopter pad, featured nearly unusable audio, as it turns out MAGA YouTubers do not have quite the same technical abilities as broadcast television networks.

The problem for Trump is that there is no way for him to declare victory. He’s not making any demands of CNN (or Politico or MS NOW, for that matter). He’s a dedicated cable news viewer, and it means he’ll get that much less coverage on the network. It also has become the first time the television networks have banded together to refuse to provide pool coverage, which sets a precedent if he chooses to go after another network.

And with Trump’s political fortunes waning and the likelihood of Democratic control of at least one chamber of Congress constraining him in his last two years of office, it’s not likely his position will get any stronger any time soon. Trump’s tantrum toward CNN and the other outlets may be a precursor of more to come and a White House that retreats to bunker mode. There’s precedent for that. In the aftermath of the 2020 election, Trump shut himself away, holding few, if any, public events and simply putting out as his schedule the boilerplate: “President Trump will work from early in the morning until late in the evening. He will make many calls and have many meetings.”

Needless to say, Trump’s stewardship of the nation during that period was not exactly his finest hour.
news.summary: He really did used to be good at this.

Americans are frustrated with the direction the country is headed as the midterm elections approach — an atmosphere that typically blows up on the party in power.

This “Drive to Decision Day” covered one-third of the most closely contested House races in the nation and two key Senate races. news.title: Shahbal Warns Ruto Against ODM “Cancer” Spreading to UDA
news.text:
Businessman Suleiman Shahbal has urged President William Ruto to prevent any political maneuvering within the ODM party from spilling over and undermining his UDA party, warning that such interference could trigger its collapse.

Speaking on Monday, September 28, Shahbal said ODM has adopted a practice of allocating party tickets based on personal closeness or friendship with the party leader, as well as on who pays more. He described the trend as a “cancer” that has consumed the party.

Shahbal further claimed that the approach helped cost the late former Prime Minister Raila Odinga the presidency in 2022, and he cautioned Ruto not to tolerate similar behavior.

“I am telling the President, William Ruto, while you are working with ODM, be careful that the cancer of ODM does not affect your party as well.

“What have those shenanigans of pushing leaders because of friendship or giving them tickets because they paid more for them done? Raila lost the presidency in Nyanza and other ODM strongholds because the people did not come out to vote. After all, politicians who got tickets did not mobilise them,” he said.

Shahbal voiced his frustration with ODM’s decision to remove Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna and Embakasi East MP Babu Owino from the party. He claimed that the move followed a plan to push him out, but he warned that he would not leave quietly.

Shahbal also hinted that he may form a new political party based in Kenya’s Coast region, which he said would break away from the dominance of large parties. He added that people in the region should be free to select their own leaders.

The businessman, who recently said he plans to run for the Mombasa governorship seat in the 2027 General Election despite Ruto’s advice, said he would not immediately choose between the government and the United Opposition. Instead, he said he will wait for both sides to clearly explain what they intend to do for the region.

He further cautioned the Opposition against relying on slogans, drawing a comparison with U.S. elections in 2024.

“It reminds me of Kamala Harris, campaign in the US: ‘Trump is corrupt, Trump is a thief, Trump is a womaniser’. Now Trump is the President. That strategy is not going to work,” he said.

news.title: Pennsylvania School District Forced to Rescind Policy to Hide Kids’ Gender Confusion from Parents
news.text:
Just to the west of Philadelphia sits largely middle-class and upper-middle-class Chester County, which still falls within the Philly metropolitan area. People aspire to live there, to buy houses there, and to raise their families there. It’s generally regarded as more affluent, safer, and offering a higher quality of life than living in the city of Philadelphia.

The county had once been reliably red politically, but now it’s considered a blue suburban area. Roughly 41% of the total registered voters in the county are Democrats; approximately 39% are Republicans. Independents make up the other roughly 20%.

It’s not so much the data on registrations as much as how the people, both Democrat and Republican, vote in the county. It’s solidly blue. In presidential elections, Kamala Harris won the county by over 14 points in 2024; Joe Biden carried the county by 17 points over President Donald Trump in 2020. In 2016, Hillary Clinton beat Trump in the county by 9 points.

So, in the spirit of you get what you vote for, parents in Chester County have been kept out of the loop by schools and their staffs on children’s “social transitions.” In other words, if your child is gender-confused and either considering transitioning, or in the midst of transitioning, Chester County Intermediate Unit 24 (CCIU) School District had policies in place to hide that information from you.

According to its website, the CCIU provides special education services to the 12 school districts in Chester County, which “includes services to nearly 86,000 school students and over 6,000 educators.”

More to the point, the district had maintained policy 103.2, which mandated that teachers hide in-school transitioning from students’ parents. It stated that, “Intermediate Unit personnel should not disclose information that may reveal a student’s transgender status or gender nonconforming presentation to others, including the student’s parents/guardians and/or other Intermediate Unit personnel, unless legally required to do so or unless the student has authorized such disclosure.”

Pretty clear, right? CCIU was not finished.

Transgender and gender nonconforming students have the right to discuss and express their gender identity and expression openly and to decide when, with whom, and how much to share such private information.When contacting the parent/guardian of a transgender or gender nonconforming student, Intermediate Unit personnel should use the student’s legal name and the pronoun corresponding to the student’s gender assigned at birth unless the student or parent/guardian has specified otherwise...When communicating with parents/guardians of transgender or gender nonconforming students, Intermediate Unit employees will refrain from the use of gender pronouns and refer to the student by name whenever practicable.The Intermediate Unit does not condone the intentional and/or persistent refusal to respect a student’s consistently asserted gender identity, or inappropriate release of information regarding a student’s transgender or gender nonconforming status. Such conduct shall be a violation of this Board policy, the policy stated.

It’s pretty clear that this policy not only prohibited staff from disclosing information on transitioning students, but also embedded in the policy itself was explicit coaching on exactly how to keep parents in the dark.

Usually policies detail the “what” of a situation, but not always the “how.” This policy went there and then some. The policy then very clearly instructed school district staff on implementation:

Based on the policy, the District requires that: a) Staff must affirm a student’s gender dysphoria by always utilizing a student’s preferred name and pronouns, based exclusively on a student’s, not their parents’ request;b) Staff cannot inform parents that their child has requested a different name and pronouns at school and must affirmatively hide that information if the parents are not already aware of that information; andc) Any District staff member who does not comply with the policy and practice will face disciplinary action.

Of course, the sorts of things that go unsaid any time a school district enacts a policy like this are how much latitude teachers and staff have on influencing children to question their own sexual identities. They’d prefer to pretend that sort of thing never happens and that these minors come up with the idea to transition all by themselves.

A U.S. Supreme Court ruling changed things

In a landmark SCOTUS case in 2026, Mirabelli v. Bonta, both parents and teachers challenged California state policies that required schools to keep information about students’ gender transitioning confidential from parents unless the students consented. These policies were very similar to the one at CCIU in Pennsylvania.

The parents sued over being excluded from any knowledge and decisions regarding their own kids’ gender confusion at school. These policies had been followed in California regardless of the parents’ religious values and beliefs, and the desire on the part of parents to be a part of their children’s mental healthcare.

But it wasn’t just the parents. Teachers joined the lawsuit because they did not want to be compelled to use the students’ new “preferred pronouns” and names at school, especially when they knew that the parents were in the dark and would have objected.

The primary holding of the Supreme Court was that the state of California cannot prevent schools from telling parents about their children’s efforts to engage in gender transitioning at school without the children's consent, or require that schools use children’s preferred names and pronouns regardless of their parents’ wishes. SCOTUS ruled that all of this is unconstitutional.

Two issues were at play. The court decided that the state’s policies were a First Amendment issue. The court ruled that the policies “likely trigger strict scrutiny” because they could interfere with a parents’ right to guide his or her children on their religious upbringing. These school policies were seen as an intrusion on this.

The other issue was one of “substantive due process” under the Fourteenth Amendment, which centers in this case on parental authority over their children’s upbringing. In other words, and this may be an over-simplification, but in a battle between who the children belong to – the state or the parents – the Constitution sides with the parents.

Some good news

In the wake of the SCOTUS decision, the Independence Law Center and the Alliance Defending Freedom sent a letter to the CCIU on behalf of an unidentified parent or set of parents of a child impacted by this policy. On May 11, Jeremy Samek, a lawyer for the Independence Law Center, sent a letter to CCIU explicitly calling for the district to rescind its policy 103.2 in light of the SCOTUS ruling.

We often joke about sending a “strongly worded letter” as an ineffectual tactic, but in this case, it was more than “strongly worded.” Samek’s letter used case law and the facts to paint the CCIU into a legal corner. He demanded not only that the policy be rescinded, but that the district actively communicate to all teachers that prior guidance on keeping gender identification confidential be disregarded.

And in a thinly veiled threat of possible litigation, he requested the district place a “litigation hold” on email records, documentation, social media accounts, and other data that reference the CCIU’s policy on gender issues.

That led to the CCIU’s decision at a board meeting on Sept. 16 to rescind that policy. PJ Media reached out to the Independence Law Center’s Randall Wenger, the Law Center’s chief counsel. He said that the SCOTUS decision in California paved the way for this district and others to change their policies.

“As a general matter, school districts want their policies to comply with the law,” Wenger said. “In light of the Supreme Court’s decision in Mirabelli v. Bonta and the (president’s) Executive Order on this issue, districts that encourage staff to conceal a child’s social transition from parents face significant legal risk.”

Of course, CCIU was not alone. According to the national nonprofit organization, Defending Education, across the country there are 1,219 school districts that still maintain similar policies. This covers 21,352 schools and a total of 12.3 million students. So, even with the SCOTUS ruling, some schools and school districts still need to be dragged kicking and screaming into constitutional compliance.

news.text: Former Obama advisers who host the "Pod Save America" podcast spoke Friday about the purported reasons some major Democratic donors are holding back money as the party sees encouraging signs ahead in November's midterm elections. Tommy Vietor replied, "I think those spending restraints compared to the opportunity are why you're starting to hear some, you know, sort of operatives and candidates like voicing concern and frustration that some of the traditional like big, big donors of the Democratic Party, are not viewing this as the generational opportunity that it could be." Vietor proposed that if the results of this midterm election resemble recent special elections where Democrats overperformed, "it is like truly a historic opportunity to win statewide races, congressional races, down-ballot, up and down. And it just feels like a moment when all the biggest donors in the party should be pushing all their chips in the table as aggressively as possible and not holding back for — I don't know what reason — Trump bothering them?" "Yeah, I think there has been a huge shift in the funding approach ... in the large donor community since 2024," Pfeiffer said. "Part of it is people still angry about how that election went and feeling like they lit a billion dollars on fire in that election, which is a fair quibble in some ways." "There are a lot of people who are very afraid of being targeted by Trump like that just that your business is going to be targeted," he continued. "You're going to have all of a sudden, you're going to the FBI is going to show up at your door. You're going to have regulatory scrutiny you wouldn't have before. And so that has limited money." CASH-STRAPPED DNC SHELLED OUT MORE THAN $800K TO NON-VOTING TERRITORIES LIKE VIRGIN ISLANDS WHILE IN DEBT Pfeiffer argued further that this midterm election could possibly lead to a scenario where "you're looking at one of the largest swings in American history, something where Democrats could pick up races we've never even thought possible," he said. "We've been using 2006 as like the most relevant example of an election because it's you know, it's an unpopular president, unpopular war, all of that. But it very well could be a little more like '94, where everything changes where it's a realigning election." Democratic consultant Julian Epstein rejected the podcasters' comments. "It's always funny to me how these group think 'insiders' parrot one another, even when they're 'consensus' is obviously wrong. The truth is that the so-called 'blue tsunami' is very likely overstated. news.title: The schizophrenic Washington Post
news.text:
The newspaper across town, which presumes to be a paper of record for the whole country, has a little problem: It is schizophrenic and sex-obsessed.

It needs a couch visit with Sigmund Freud, or at least Dr. Phil.

When Amazon founder Jeff Bezos bought The Washington Post in 2013, he unaccountably let the inmates run the asylum, with progressive propaganda permeating every section, including sports.

Last year, Mr. Bezos, a capitalist who made his billions in America’s free market system, had had enough. He reined in the editorial section, which had lurched so far left that it sounded like the Soviet Union’s Pravda, or today’s Democratic Socialists of America.

On Feb. 26, 2025, the Post newsroom got a public memo from Mr. Bezos informing them that the opinion section would henceforth defend “personal liberties and free markets.”

And so it has, at least in most editorials. The paper still has leftist columnists. But it has added conservative opinion content that would not be out of place in The Washington Times or The Wall Street Journal.

Oh, the horror. Editorial page editor David Shipley resigned immediately, followed by several other opinion staff members. It also cost the Post 75,000 online subscribers, on top of the exodus of 200,000 to 300,000 subscribers who canceled when the Post declined to endorse Kamala Harris for president in 2024.

Mr. Bezos did not seem to mind and continued bankrolling the paper, which has been losing as much as $100 million a year.

The problem is that the housecleaning stopped too soon. The paper’s feature and news sections still read today like they are edited by Hasan Piker, Greta Thunberg, and RuPaul.

Here’s a headline on a Foreign Policy magazine story the Post ran on Sept. 17: “By nearly every metric, the U.S. is losing the Iran war.”

Meanwhile, not a day passes without the Post pouring gasoline on the nation’s divisions. If there is no recent George Floyd, they reach back to remind readers about how awful America has always been, because, you know, straight white people.

You would think the food section would be safe, at least. You would be wrong.

On Sept. 2, food critic Tim Carmen did a two-page hit piece on Chick-fil-A and its chicken-and-waffle sandwich. He says the dish “became a staple on plantations, where enslaved cooks prepared what became known as a ‘Virginia breakfast.'”

He then asks, “Does this dish deserve to be on the menu of a chain with a history of intolerance?”

Say what? Oh, right. Chick-fil-A’s president defended marriage as the union of a man and a woman back in 2019, and the chain supports Christian charities.

Even the Post’s comics pages are woke. The Sunday section features Doonesbury, which stopped being funny years ago and is fully devoted to Trump Derangement Syndrome.

Six Chix, a badly drawn strip by six rotating leftist women, last February featured a panel showing a brick, with the words, “Iconic symbols of resistance.” Wow. They’re a riot.

A couple of weeks ago, the Post’s chief arts critic, Philip Kennicott, wrote a scathing piece about the Trump administration’s efforts to get leftist propaganda out of the Smithsonian Institution.

“Never has the nation more urgently needed to focus on key issues, like climate change and its long history of racial, ethnic, and class division,” he wrote.

Yes, keep pouring on the gasoline. Upon reading Mr. Kennicott’s screed, I easily imagined him out on a curb with other grizzled, privileged hippies, yelling “No kings!”

On March 1, the Ask Sahaj column in the Style section fielded a question from a woman who wrote, “I have a deep fear my brown skin and hijab will make me unattractive to other people.”

Sahaj Kaur Kohli’s answer begins: “You need to accept that the messaging about beauty standards you’ve internalized is rooted in white supremacy and colonialism.”

The Post also carries a column by Shane O’Neill, whose purpose seems to be to evangelize for sexual promiscuity.

A newly divorced woman asks him how much sex she should have. He answers: “Keep on having as much sex as you want. … You’re no longer monogamous! Hooray!! As a gay guy, I’m used to getting tested every three months.”

He recommends using condoms or taking a daily pill to ward off HIV, and says, “If you’re not interested in a committed monogamous relationship, finding one or two (or 16) ‘regulars’ can significantly cut down on time spent looking for new partners.” How practical.

In another column. he counsels a 29-year-old woman who says she is a virgin but has decided she is a lesbian. He tells her to have sex and not worry because, “Virginity is a construct. It has historically been used to control and extract monetary value from women’s bodies. … the concept has no value.”

The devil himself could not have put it better. It sounds a lot like a sermon by Texas U.S. Senate Democratic candidate James Talarico’s wacky pastor.

Moving on to films, a July 31 review by Katie Walsh via the Tribune News Service of the movie “I Want Your Sex” gives it three and a half stars –- nearly a perfect score. Ms. Walsh lauds filmmaker Gregg Araki for his “message to Gen Z, which is to have some sex already. The kids could stand to be a little more kinky, a little more queer, to get out of their heads and into their bodies.”

I don’t know about you, but I wouldn’t let anybody impressionable near this newspaper until it gets over its schizophrenia.

This column was first published at the Washington Times.

news.title: Gaza – a convenient excuse to hate Jews
news.text:
Who would have thought that a day on which 1,200 Jews were murdered – the largest one-day Jewish death toll since the Holocaust – would lead to an upsurge of antisemitism?

It used to be medieval mobs shouting, “Death to the Jews” and the Nazis promising to make Europe “Judenrein” – free of Jews. Now, it’s “Free Palestine,” the new “Heil Hitler.”

news.title: Anti-South Asian ‘hate speech’ has exploded online in US, report finds  - Jamaica Inquirer – Daily Jamaica
news.text:
Hate speech against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis in the United States has risen sharply online, according to a report that traces the surge to US President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and rhetoric, economic anxiety, and the South Asian community’s growing visibility in US life.

The report, titled “The Rising Tide of Anti-South Asian Hate in the United States”, by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate (CSOH), published on Sunday, found that the monthly volume of hate towards South Asians in the US on the social media platform X rose 240 percent between January 2024 and June 2026, from 12,904 posts to 43,843.

Researchers identified more than 542,000 hateful posts on the platform between January 2025 and June 2026 alone towards people from South Asia living in the US, with five of the six highest-volume months falling at the end of that period.

The researchers used the United Nations definition of hate speech. They tracked recurring anti-South Asian slurs and narratives online, reviewing posts to exclude criticism that did not meet the UN threshold.

They found that nearly half of the hate posts on X accused South Asians of invading the US, stealing jobs or threatening the country demographically, while the derogatory slur “pajeet” and its variants showed up in 30 percent of hateful posts on X and 45 percent on fringe platforms.

Posts depicting South Asians as dirty or unhygienic grew by 171 percent on X, “the fastest of all narratives”.

The hate frequently collapsed South Asian ethnic and religious groups into one, with Indians, Pakistanis and Bangladeshis conflated with one another, and Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Christians also treated as a monolith.

So why now?

Racism against Indians, Bangladeshis and Pakistanis has a long history in the US, but researchers argue the current surge reflects a confluence of longstanding prejudices and new political and economic pressures.

The report points to the H-1B visa programme, which allows US employers to hire skilled foreign workers, as a major flashpoint. Indians account for more than 70 percent of H-1B visa holders, and researchers linked several spikes in anti-South Asian hate to political fights over the programme, such as when Trump imposed a $100,000 payment requirement on certain new H-1B petitions in September 2025.

“Such actions serve a powerful symbolic function, in the bargain reinforcing the hostility of Trump’s base toward South Asians,” said the report.

The report makes the same argument about the administration’s rhetoric, highlighting Trump’s speech at an AI summit in July 2025, in which he criticised US technology companies for outsourcing jobs to India, after which researchers saw a sharp spike in anti-South Asian rhetoric online.

As more recent examples, the report points to a since-deleted September 2026 Department of Homeland Security post titled “Transformers: Age of Deportations”, featuring a Sikh man identified as “Mr Singh” and telling him to “get off our roads”.

Days later, the Department of Education posted “Make College Football Great Again”, after Texas Republican Bo French had complained about the presence of South Asians at a University of Texas football game.

The report argues that such rhetoric reinforces the idea of South Asians as outsiders who “can never truly belong in the country”.

From ‘model minority’ to job thieves

Economic resentment is another factor, researchers wrote, with the success of some South Asians increasingly being weaponised against them.

Indian Americans once stereotyped as a “model minority” are now portrayed as “opportunists and cheats”, and South Asians are used more broadly as a scapegoat for anger over jobs and the economy.

This comes as South Asians have become increasingly visible in US politics, from former Vice President Kamala Harris and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani to Vice President JD Vance’s wife, Usha Vance, and politician Vivek Ramaswamy. The report documents racist attacks against figures across party lines and highlights how, for example, Mamdani’s primary and mayoral victories triggered spikes in anti-South Asian and Islamophobic abuse.

Researchers say both trends are now also tied up with “anxieties on the part of the majority about loss of status”, and feed the “Great Replacement Theory”, a conspiracy about the white population in Western countries being replaced by an orchestrated takeover.

Social media has also turned those narratives into targeted harassment.

Researchers found X accounts doxxing South Asians accused of taking jobs or committing visa fraud, while influencers have confronted people at their homes and workplaces and posted the encounters online. Doxxing refers to exposing a person’s private details, such as their home address, online.

In one example, right-wing influencer Sara Gonzalez posted a video to more than half a million followers in which the report says she harassed a South Asian person she accused of exploiting the H-1B programme.

Meanwhile, generative AI has made that content even easier to produce, researchers say, depicting South Asians as “filthy and unclean, sexually predatory, culturally backward, or a demographic threat”.

While the report tracks hate largely through what is happening online, researchers write that online hate “does not exist in isolation from offline forms of hostility”. It cites a July incident in which an Indian Muslim mall employee in Utah was repeatedly stabbed in an attack that federal prosecutors charged as a hate crime. In September, a Sikh truck driver was stabbed 17 times at a Wyoming truck stop.

“Online and offline hate can reinforce one another”, the researchers wrote, “as narratives, stereotypes, and forms of demonization move between digital platforms, political discourse, media, and everyday life”.

news.title: White House airs more taxpayer-funded ads promoting Trump
news.text:
The federal government has spent at least $1.7 million to air three different TV ads featuring President Donald Trump in recent days, according to an estimate from AdImpact, which tracks and analyzes political ad spending across television, digital and connected TV channels.

Critics say the ads could violate federal propaganda law. The White House has defended them as “public service announcements” and drawn comparisons to past examples of administrations that created PSA's to highlight new drug coverage under Medicare and signups for the Affordable Care Act exchanges. 

The latest ad features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing “the final battle” against "the deep state,” “the globalists,” and “the sick political class that hates our country.”

The president is seen glaring directly at the camera as his voiceover vows to “rout the fake news media” and “liberate America from these villains once and for all."

The same video was shared by Trump three years ago when he was out of office and a declared candidate for president. The audio is taken from a Trump campaign stop in Michigan in June 2023.

A search of the monitoring service TVEyes indicates the ad ran at least twice over the weekend on the Fox Broadcasting Network -- once during college football on Saturday and again Sunday on "Fox News Sunday."

Another ad that aired Sunday on NBC's "Meet the Press" shows images of Trump at an event at Mt. Rushmore celebrating the country's 250th birthday in which he celebrates "only the beginning of the golden age of America."

An ad aired last week showed Trump boasting about his record and vowing the United States "will never be a communist country." That ad ran repeatedly during the week on conservative cable news channels Fox News and Newsmax across several media markets, according to AdImpact, a media buying and tracking firm. 

Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee who would help lead congressional oversight efforts if his party retakes the House this fall, condemned the first ad after it aired last week.

"This may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes," Raskin wrote. "It is a Hatch Act violation for any government employees who worked on it or used government resources to make it. It is blatantly unethical under numerous federal ethics provisions proscribing the use of government resources for political campaigns."

The Hatch Act restricts certain political activities by federal employees and by some state, Washington, D.C., and local government workers who are involved or work in federally funded programs.

Democratic Sen. Maggie Hassan requested information on the first ad from White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, asking for details about how the ad was produced and the source of the federal funds used to air it.

Some Republicans have criticized the ads as well.

Brinker Harding, the Republican candidate in Nebraska's 2nd District, represented by retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon, and won by Kamala Harris by five points in 2024, issued a statement condemning the taxpayer-funded ads.

"America is $40 trillion dollars in debt, and Nebraskans are struggling to make ends meet. We should be laser focused on spending the taxpayers’ hard earned dollars wisely, not funding political TV advertisements with their money," Harding posted on X.

Republican Sen. John Kennedy criticized the first ad after it aired, saying that public funds shouldn’t be used for such a cause. 

"I don't think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves," he said. "Now, the White House sees it differently, but I think there ought to be a rule that you can't -- well, there probably is a rule -- you can't spend public money to promote yourself."

White House Communications Director Steven Cheung defended the administration’s ads on Sunday. 

“Don’t let the Fake News get away with their lies about our epic Public Service Announcements that have been running on tv,” Cheung wrote. 

Asked on Sunday about the ad that appears to be a copy of the 2024 campaign ad, the White House said in a statement that the “public service announcements are about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

It added, “The ad is educational and unapologetically patriotic. We should be proud of our country.”

A White House official also defended the ads as “clearly not political” and asserted that Trump “is not on the ballot and the ads don’t have a call to action,” though Trump has repeatedly encouraged voters to “pretend” that he is on the ballot.

Cheung supplied a White House fact sheet on the ads highlighting President Woodrow Wilson’s efforts to bolster support for World War I in a campaign that used taxpayer funds to manipulate public opinion and shape news coverage.

While it birthed the classic American image of Uncle Sam saying “I Want You for U.S. Army,” much of the work of the Creel Committee remains infamous -- it has been said by historians to have inspired the propaganda efforts of Hitler’s government in Nazi Germany.

news.title: Kamala Harris' Former Campaign Chair Won't Commit to Backing Her in 2028
news.text: Mitch Landrieu, the former New Orleans mayor who co-chaired Kamala Harris' 2024 presidential campaign, says he is thinking about running for president himself. Asked whether he would support another Harris run, he declined to say yes. "I like her very much. I enjoyed serving with her. I thought she ran a good campaign under very difficult circumstances," Landrieu told Carlo Versano in an interview on Newsweek's The 1600 podcast. He stopped short of an endorsement though. "If she wants to run, everybody should run. I don't think we ought to be in the business of telling people what to do or what not to do," he said. "I think the country is looking for something different and something new." He closed his answer with advice for any 2028 hopeful. "If you feel like you got in your heart and your soul you feel you have something to give to the country, get out there and let the voters tell you whether or not you get to stay on the island." Responding to a question about whether he was mulling a presidential bid, Landrieu confirmed it. "I am thinking about it," he said. "I'll make a decision at the appropriate time." Watch: The 1600 The South as the Battleground Landrieu, a Democrat who also served as Louisiana's lieutenant governor and as President Joe Biden's infrastructure coordinator, said he cares more about what ordinary people can do than about who holds the White House. "Democracy is not self-operating," he said. "A president alone will not save us." He argued that neither the courts nor Congress can be counted on to check President Donald Trump. Republicans in Congress, in his view, are not restraining the president the way a Republican majority did with Richard Nixon. "The senators are not coming. The congressmen are not coming. The only people who can save this country are the people." Landrieu joined the show to talk about The Long Play, a docuseries he hosts for Crooked Media that travels through Southern states ahead of the midterms. The series rests on the idea that the South is where American politics is headed. He pointed to population movement as the driver. "People are moving out of California, or maybe not necessarily into Florida anymore but from Florida to North Carolina, or people are moving from New Jersey down to Tennessee," Landrieu said. "When people move, things change." Democrats, he said, have paid a price for writing off the region. "There has been a massive disinvestment politically in trying to build things in the South," Landrieu said. "If you want people to vote for you, you have to go see them, even if you've been losing." In Texas, he said, the Senate race between Democratic candidate James Talarico and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, could be closer than many expect. Landrieu attended a Talarico rally in Laredo and met people there who had voted for Trump three times and planned to back Talarico. "They said, we're very disappointed in the president. We voted for him three times. He said he was gonna do two things, stay out of wars and reduce our costs. He didn't do either one of those things," Landrieu said. The polls back him up. Siena College has Talarico ahead of Paxton 49 percent to 43 percent in a survey taken September 8 to 11, and Emerson College has it much tighter at 47 to 46. Emerson also found that Hispanic voters in Texas, who went for Trump in 2024, now lean Talarico by 15 points, 54 percent to 39 percent. On his home state, Landrieu was more cautious. Louisiana, he said, will be one of the last Southern states to shift toward Democrats, along with Mississippi. "My honest assessment is that it's a little bit harder than all the other states right now." A Warning on Litmus Tests Voters no longer sort themselves neatly by party, according to Landrieu. Working-class Americans feel the system is rigged against them, he said, and are losing patience with politicians who speak to them simply as Republicans or Democrats. Trump's numbers reflect that broader frustration, Landrieu warned. Most polling averages now put his approval at 33 percent and disapproval at 61 percent nationally, giving him a net rating of minus 28. In July, his net rating was minus 19. He also had a message for the far left of his own party. "If you're not with me a hundred percent, you're not with me at all. In my opinion, that is a losing proposition, politically, spiritually, economically and for our country," Landrieu said. As some Democrats have reconsidered or distanced themselves from positions associated with the progressive politics of the late 2010s, Landrieu has not backed away from one of his most controversial decisions as mayor. In 2017, he ordered the removal of four Confederate monuments in New Orleans, a move that drew fierce opposition at the time. Nearly a decade later, he said he has no regrets. “I'd do it twice as fast and I'd do more if I could,” he said, calling the monuments “a lie.” Landrieu also defended the Biden administration's infrastructure law against Democrats who say the White House was too slow to get projects built before the 2024 election. He said the administration pushed $800 billion out the door in under a year and a half and started 73,000 projects. He acknowledged the political payoff was limited. "Politically, it didn't help very much, I agree with that," Landrieu said. "But in terms of a good piece of public policy that's really gonna impact the future of the country, I stand by it." news.title: ABC13 looks at why there's been a lack of debates in statewide races on November ballot
news.text:
HOUSTON, Texas (KTRK) -- We are 36 days from Election Day, and something is missing from the top-of-the-ballot campaigns: none of them have debated one another.

It's not unheard of for candidates to decline debates. But it's rare in modern Texas politics to have no debates for the U.S. Senate, governor, and lieutenant governor, especially given that some of the current candidates have debated in the past.

James Talarico is running for the U.S. Senate against Ken Paxton. He's agreed to debate, but Paxton has not.

In fact, Paxton has never debated an opponent as a statewide candidate.

Gina Hinojosa has offered to debate Governor Greg Abbott. Abbott has not reciprocated. It's a first for Abbott-who debated Wendy Davis in 2014 during his first run for Governor, Lupe Valdez in 2018, and Beto O'Rourke four years ago.

Lt. Governor Dan Patrick has not said yes to a debate against Vikki Goodwin. He has not debated an opponent since 2014, when he faced off against then-Lt. Governor David Dewhurst in the primary and Leticia Van de Putte in the general election 12 years ago.

"It's unfortunate that we're not having them this year," Nancy Sims, a University of Houston political science lecturer and a veteran of political campaigns, told ABC13. "The largest percentage of voters consider themselves independent, and debates really are a tool candidates can use to persuade voters in their favor."

Ted Cruz is not on the ticket this year, but he debated opponents in all three of his races for the US Senate. In a close 2018 race, he debated Beto O'Rourke twice. And John Cornyn debated MJ Hegar six years ago.

"I honestly believe that a debate would empower their opponents further and that they're giving them free publicity if they deign to debate them," Sims said.

Do debates matter? Well, that's been up for debate for quite a while.

A Harvard study of 60 years of televised debates in different countries found they really did not affect Election Day. But Sims points to two years ago, and the debate between then-President Biden and President Trump. Biden's poor performance did make a difference.

"It caused him to drop out of the race. It caused Kamala Harris to come into the race. That debate became a defining moment for the 2024 presidential election," Sims said.

You can still see all of these candidates, Republicans and Democrats, in their television ads, online, or at in-person events across the state, but because the three Republicans at the top of the ballot have not agreed to debate, you may not get to see them live and unfiltered on the same stage with their Democratic opponents.

news.title: Trump Was Asked What He Really Thinks About Women In Leadership — And He Just Said The Quiet Part Out Loud
news.text:
President Donald Trump did not mince words when asked about the notion of women in charge of governments and former President Barack Obama’s suggestion that the world would improve under female leadership.

During an event with historian Doris Kearns Goodwin at Salem State University last week, Obama remarked that during his time in office, he “sometimes fantasized about, if you put women in charge of every government for like two years, and then just kind of saw, all right, how are things going?”

“I have a strong belief that things would ― they wouldn’t be perfect ― but they’d be better. I’m confident about that,” he added. 

While speaking to the press on Saturday, Trump responded to a question about the 44th president’s claim.

“Barack Obama just said if you put women in charge of every government for two years, things would be better. Do you buy that?” one reporter asked. 

“It’s a ridiculous ― I love women, I think they’re great, but what a ridiculous statement that is, right? Even you would say that,” Trump replied. 

Experts in politics and gender studies say the president’s remarks in the interview are quite telling. When asked about the president’s remarks, the White House referred HuffPost to Trump’s original comment.

“Obama is empirically right that the world would look radically different if women were in charge,” Caroline Heldman, a professor of political science and the chair of gender, women and sexuality studies at Occidental College, told HuffPost. “Decades of research finds that women world leaders have different policy priorities, governing styles, ethics, foreign policy approaches and responses to crises than men leaders.”

She noted that women officeholders tend to give more attention to issues like healthcare, education, childcare, parental leave, pay equity and violence against women.

“They place greater emphasis on collaboration, consensus-building and cross-party coalitions; demonstrate lower levels of corruption; are more likely to favor diplomacy, multilateral cooperation and humanitarian aid; and are more effective in reaching peace agreements,” Heldman added. “During COVID-19, women-led countries acted earlier, followed expert guidance more closely, communicated more clearly and saw better health outcomes.”

She was careful to note that none of this is about biology or innate differences ― but rather stems from “gendered socialization, the expectations placed on women leaders and the pressure women face to prove their competence in male-dominated institutions.”

Heldman also presented a thought experiment to get a sense of how different the world could be if women were in charge. 

“Imagine how different the U.S. would look if half of our presidents from the start had been women,” she said. “How would the U.S. be different if Hillary Clinton were elected in 2016? I assure you that had Kamala Harris been elected in 2024, we would not be in a foreign quagmire in Iran, we would not be paying $6.36 in California for gas, we would not be paying an average of $1,700 in extra household costs from new tariffs and we would actually know what’s in the Epstein files.”

Political scientist Shauna Shames, an associate professor at Rutgers University-Camden who studies gender and American politics, offered two reads of Trump’s remarks.

“The less charitable read ... is that Trump may indeed love women, but for certain things only, and not when they wield political power,” she said. “When they do, he tends to give them pretty awful nicknames and do a lot of mocking and ridicule. It is the first refuge of an insecure man.”

Throughout his time in the spotlight, Trump has lobbed several insults at women, from calling leaders like Hillary Clinton and Kamala Harris “nasty” to going after celebrities like Jessica Chastain (“not hot”), Bette Midler (“extremely unattractive”), Stormy Daniels (“horseface”) and Rosie O’Donnell (“fat” and “a pig”).

And then there are all of his attacks on female reporters ― including telling Bloomberg’s Catherine Lucey “Quiet, piggy!”, dismissing CNN’s Kaitlan Collins as “very dumb and unhappy,” dubbing Maggie Haberman “Maggot Hagerman” and calling The New York Times’ Katie Rogers “ugly.” 

“Donald Trump’s claim that he loves women is not borne out by his dismissal of their superior leadership, nor the reports of serious sexual abuse against him,” Heldman emphasized.

On the question of whether the world would be a better place with women in charge, there is some nuance worth exploring, said Laurie Essig, a professor of gender, sexuality and feminist studies at Middlebury College.

“Many of us like to fantasize about a world without men or where men are subordinate to women because the Epstein files and the Cornell rape case and the current misogyny and rape culture of the manosphere and Trumpism ― ‘If we just put women in charge, wouldn’t it be better?’” she said. “And the short answer is: It’s complicated.”

She noted that within feminist movements, some have held that women are innately better than men, while others have argued the real goal should be transforming systems for all people.

“There’s also broad agreement that in the current moment of strongly misogynist culture and politics, men and boys are being conditioned to lack empathy and believe that might makes right whereas women and girls are socialized to be aware of others and act in ways that are less harmful,” Essig said. “But if you leave all the power structures in place that allow domination by those with the most power, then eventually those with power would probably use it to harm others with little empathy.”

That said, her ultimate conclusion landed closer to Obama’s.

“I say yeah, I’m with President Obama. Let’s create a world where we put women in charge,” she said. “Some research shows that women leaders are in fact more cooperative and more likely to enact policies that benefit children and families. But that’s because they’ve been socialized as women. So perhaps if we socialized men and boys to care deeply about others in this hypothetical world, then they too could be president one day.”

Kari Winter, a professor of global gender and sexuality studies at the University at Buffalo placed Trump’s dismissal in a broader context.

“According to the International Committee of the Red Cross, military conflicts are escalating globally to the tune of approximately 130 armed conflicts across 60 countries,” she said. “Donald Trump’s administration responds by calling for testosterone shots and greater lethality. After launching a reckless war of choice against Iran, Trump in his United Nations speech brought enormous shame on the United States by threatening the ‘annihilation’ of an ancient civilization.”

Winter was equally pointed about Trump’s track record more broadly.

“Listening to the doomsday scenarios that Trump and his bombastic ilk casually, stupidly and unimaginatively spout day after day, the world can observe that Trump excels at generating horrific new problems,” she said. “At the same time, it appears that he has never met a problem that he was capable of solving.”

As for Trump’s specific response to Obama’s comments, there was a clear familiar pattern.

“Given the dire state of the male-dominated world, Barack Obama’s invitation for us to imagine a world led by women makes a lot of sense. But Trump cannot imagine a better world,” Winter said. “In his nine-second response to the reporter’s question, he hits three of his habitual knee-jerk notes: disrespecting women, demeaning reporters, and dismissing as ‘ridiculous’ any idea to which he cannot formulate a reasoned response. His statement reveals nothing new. It hits the same sour notes we’ve heard time and again, ad nauseam.”

Shames also offered what she called an “extremely charitable read” of Trump’s “unbelievably sexist and idiotic remark” about women in government by examining the role of privilege in shaping his worldview. 

“Trump’s response to the reporter’s question surprises me not at all,” she explained. “One of the nicest things about having privilege ― and Trump has generally had just about every kind you can think of ― is that you don’t see it. So you don’t generally think about people who don’t get it. So the widespread and systematic exclusion of women from political power, not just here but generally worldwide, is probably never something that has entered Trump’s pampered, highly protected mind.”

She questioned whether Trump has any grasp of (or interest in) the historical barriers women have faced in political life.

“If I spouted the statistics about how little political power women have compared to their proportion of the population, he would call it fake news, I am sure,” Shames said. “And since he seems to have no understanding of history, the idea that the government itself has played no small role in preventing women from not only running for office, but doing things like serving on juries and even voting for the majority of American history would not get through to him.”
