news.title: Abdul El-Sayed Knows He's Losing — and Here's the Tell
news.text:
I'm not going to be one of those guys who scream that the polls are fake and we’re actually winning big, but I've been doing this long enough to recognize the signs that public polling is off and to notice when even the candidate knows it.

Remember Ann Selzer's infamous final Iowa poll in 2024? It showed Kamala Harris leading Donald Trump by three points. It shocked the entire country. It didn't take long to figure out that not even the Kamala campaign believed it. If her team had trusted those numbers, Kamala would have rushed to Iowa to lock down a stunning pickup. She never went. Trump went on to win the state by 13 points.

Iowa was never competitive. Ann Selzer, despite her reputation, was just wrong, wrong, wrong.

Michigan's U.S. Senate race is a different story.

It's definitely competitive, even though it probably shouldn't be. Democrats nominated socialist Abdul El-Sayed, and while most polls show him with a slight lead, he just handed us a huge sign that his campaign thinks he's behind.

El-Sayed built his political brand on Medicare for All. For years, he pushed a plan that would ban private insurance and force every American onto a single government plan. He even suggested repealing the Second Amendment and replacing it with a constitutional right to health care. What one has to do with the other, I have no idea, but make no mistake about it, this was never a side issue for him. It was the centerpiece of everything he stood for.

ICYMI: AOC's Presidential Ambitions Face a Humiliating Setback

His record on the issue goes back years and never wavers. In 2018, he argued that Michigan should replace its multiple insurance companies. The following year, he laid out exactly what his plan meant.

"Medicare-for-All is a single-payer healthcare plan," El-Sayed said in 2019. "That means that under Medicare-for-All, the federal government is the only payer."

That same year, he acknowledged that Medicare for All "eliminates your private" health care plan. He kept at it in 2020. "What Medicare for All does is it does away with the private insurance market. It now has one single payer…the government," he said. Around the same time, he declared that "Medicare for All comes in and says 'no more of this insurance industry,'" and described private insurance as a "middleman" that should be "cut out."

"We are going to create one insurer," El-Sayed promised in 2021. He also claimed his plan would eliminate private health insurance and create "one insurance program for everyone," while insisting the health insurance industry "does not need to exist" and "should not exist."

By 2022, his message hadn't budged. "I advocate for a government takeover of health insurance," he said.

Now El-Sayed is suddenly all for people staying on private insurance if they want to.

"If you would like to have a private insurer, above that, you're welcome to do that," El-Sayed says now, channeling his inner Barack Obama.

Abdul El-Sayed is a liar.El-Sayed has already called to completely eliminate private insurance at least 10 times. https://t.co/66BzAxjAXO pic.twitter.com/zuEC0B7C83— RNC Research (@RNCResearch) September 26, 2026

Abdul El-Sayed is a total fraud.He wants to ban your private health plan and force everyone on government-run healthcare.👇 pic.twitter.com/9B4JnwElQH— Republicans (@Republicans) September 23, 2026

Sorry, but if you're ahead and everything is going well, you don't flip-flop on an issue you've been consistent on for years. Candidates who like their numbers stay the course because it’s working. Nervous candidates start rewriting their records because they realize they need to appeal to middle-ground voters who will decide the election.

So it should come as no surprise that a new poll shows Republican Mike Rogers leading El-Sayed by 1.3 points.

Sure, it's one poll. But when El-Sayed is flip-flopping on his signature issue mere weeks before Election Day, it’s obvious he knows his campaign is in trouble.

news.title: Susan Collins Faces New Headwind as Maine Heating Costs Hit Record High
news.text: Senator Susan Collins is facing a new economic headwind in her reelection bid as home heating oil prices surge to a record high ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. Rising fuel prices have emerged as a key vulnerability for Republicans nationwide as they defend their majorities in both the House of Representatives and Senate, with only about 5 weeks until the midterms. Rising costs are attributed to disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, a key passageway for global oil, amid the Iran war. Collins faces a unique challenge in Maine, the state most reliant on home heating oil. More than 50 percent of Maine residents use oil as their primary heat source, according to the Northeast Gas Association, and prices have steadily increased as winter approaches, adding pressure to Mainers’ finances as they weigh whether to elect Collins to another term. Home heating prices averaged $6.02 per gallon statewide last week, according to the Maine Department of Energy Resources (DOER). That marks an increase from $3.33 per gallon one year earlier, and more conservative, rural parts of the state are facing especially high costs. The previous high was recorded in May 2022, when prices hit $5.92 per gallon as the nation grappled with a post-pandemic inflation wave. Heating costs are “always front of mind in Maine,” even in the “middle of the summer,” Mark Brewer, a professor of political science at the University of Maine in Orono, told Newsweek. “It’s cold here. Winter is long. It’s definitely a huge concern, even in years where fuel costs aren’t high. When they reach the point where they are right now, and they’re projected to go even higher, it’s definitely going to be a big issue,” he said. “No doubt about it.” Newsweek reached out to the Collins and Jackson campaigns for comment via email. Collins’ Reelection Bid Complicated by Rising Home Heating Prices Rising home heating prices threaten to complicate Collins’ reelection. She already faces a toss-up race against Democrat Troy Jackson, the former Maine Senate president, and affordability remains a central concern for voters both in Maine and across the country. The Iran war has not been popular in the polls. Trump’s approval rating has fallen after launching strikes against Tehran in February, as voters blame him for rising costs caused by the war. If voters blame Trump for rising home heating prices, Collins “is going to get some of that” heat, Brewer said. “She’s not Trump, obviously, but Trump is the president of her party, and Troy Jackson and his supporters are already making the argument that Collins is a Trump enabler, so this could definitely come back and bite her,” he said. Costs in Northern and Central Maine, which are the state’s more conservative regions, are even higher, averaging $6.05 and $6.09 per gallon, respectively. Jackson is not going to win those regions, but he could chip away at Collins’ margins there by focusing on heating prices, Brewer said. “If Troy Jackson can whittle away there, and he can do it using high heating costs as a chisel, that’s certainly going to help him,” he said. Meanwhile, Collins is likely to highlight her efforts to ensure federal support for the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP), which provides funding for low-income households’ energy costs in Maine, he said. Democrats Criticize Collins Over Heating Prices Jackson has criticized Collins over rising heating prices. “The best time to stop a war is before it starts. Susan Collins repeatedly voted to let Trump’s disastrous war in Iran continue. Now Mainers are paying through the nose for gas, diesel, and heating oil. What the hell is she good for?” he wrote in a September 17 post on X. Maine Democratic Party spokesperson Misha Linnehan also released a statement on Monday criticizing Collins’ position on the war. Collins initially voted against War Powers Resolutions that would have restricted Trump’s ability to wage war but started voting in support of those resolutions in April, citing its “clear 60-day deadline for Congress to either authorize or end U.S. involvement in foreign hostilities.” Linnehan wrote that the risks were “clear” the moment Trump began the “reckless war.” “Now, as the weather gets colder, Maine families are paying more than ever before to heat their homes, and there’s no end to the war in sight,” Linnehan wrote. Collins Presses Trump on Oil Prices Collins and Senator Angus King, a Maine independent, sent a letter to Trump last week urging him to release supply from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve to lower costs for Mainers. “Maine is particularly vulnerable to global supply shocks because our state imports much of our home heating oil. With both domestic and international supplies running low, a release from the Northeast Home Heating Oil Reserve would help ease these prices,” the letter reads. In April, Collins announced that $421 million in LIHEAP funding was released for the program, which she said provides “vital relief to thousands of Mainers” that helps them “avoid the constant worry of choosing between heating their homes and covering other basic necessities.” Susan Collins vs. Troy Jackson: What Latest Polls Show About Maine Senate Race Polls have shown a close race between Collins and Jackson. A recent poll from The New York Times, The Portland Press Herald and Siena University released on Thursday showed Collins up 3 points, 49 percent to 46 percent. It surveyed 619 likely voters from September 15 to 22. But other polls released last week showed Jackson leading Collins. Jackson led by 4 points in a University of New Hampshire poll, with 51 percent support to Collins’ 47 percent, up from July, when he led by 3 points. It surveyed 1,312 likely voters from September 17 to 21 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.7 percentage points. Another poll from the University of Massachusetts Lowell gave Jackson a 5-point lead, 48 percent to 43 percent. Among independent voters, a critical voting bloc in the Pine Tree State, he led by 8 points, 40 percent to 32 percent, with 22 percent still undecided, the poll found. Collins and Jackson were tied in an InsiderAdvantage poll, which showed them both at around 46 percent. It surveyed 1,200 likely voters from September 22 to 23, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.83 percentage points. Can Susan Collins Defy a Blue Wave? Notably, the 2020 race between Collins and Democrat Sara Gideon saw a polling error in Collins’ favor, though polling errors don't always repeat from cycle to cycle. Collins trailed Gideon in nearly every poll but ultimately outperformed the polls to hold onto the seat, even as former President Joe Biden won the state by 9 points that year. Democrats note that 2026 is likely to be a stronger national environment. Still, Maine is a difficult state to poll due to its older, rural population. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won Maine by about 7 points in 2024, but Collins has won in the past because of her personal popularity and bipartisan image. Democrats believe that a strong national environment this year could give them their best chance yet at unseating the longtime incumbent. Still, Republicans view the race as competitive and have hoped to cast Jackson as too progressive for the state. Democrats have also had a tumultuous election season in the state. Graham Platner, a progressive political newcomer whose campaign garnered national attention, was hit with sexual abuse allegations just weeks after clinching the nomination. He has denied the allegations but ultimately withdrew from the race. Jackson, who initially ran for governor but lost the primary, emerged as the new nominee during a convention in July, easily securing the required delegates to find his place on the ballot. What Do Prediction Markets Show? Prediction markets favor Jackson to flip Maine. As of Monday, he had a 61 percent chance on both Kalshi and Polymarket of winning against Collins. Prediction markets let traders buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real-money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always predict the future accurately. Why the Maine Senate Race Matters in 2026 Midterms Democrats’ path to a Senate majority runs through Maine. Democrats are increasingly hopeful about winning the Senate despite a difficult map. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control if they win every race in a seat they currently hold. Vance serves as the tiebreaker in a split Senate. To flip the Senate majority, Democrats must win every seat they currently hold, flip GOP-held seats in competitive states, and win some seats in more traditionally conservative territory. Democrats are defending seats in Trump-won states Georgia and Michigan. In addition to Maine, they view a GOP-held seat in North Carolina as a top flip opportunity. The race in New Hampshire, which backed Harris by about 3 points, is also competitive. No other Senate races are in Harris-won or single-digit Trump states, meaning Democrats must expand the Senate battleground and compete in more conservative areas if they want to win the majority. They are targeting GOP-held seats in Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas as potential states to flip. The Cook Political Report classifies those four races as tossups. What Happens Next The Maine Senate race is expected to remain one of the most competitive battlegrounds of this year’s midterms, with forecasters like the Cook Political Report and Sabato’s Crystal Ball classifying it as a pure toss-up. news.summary: Mainers are facing surging home heating prices as winter approaches, creating a new challenge for Collins' reelection bid.

news.title: 15 planes violated a temporary flight restriction over Chicago area during Trump's visit to Medinah Sunday
news.text:
Fifteen civilian planes violated a temporary flight restriction that was in place on Sunday during President Trump’s nine-hour trip to Illinois, with flares being deployed at two planes who did not initially respond to F-16 military jets flying alongside their wings.

Trump landed at O’Hare Airport at 9:40 a.m. to attend the Presidents Cup golf tournament in suburban Medinah. Air Force One was wheeled up at O’Hare at 6:40 p.m. During that time, the North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) put in place a VIP temporary flight restriction over the Chicago area. 

NORAD says 15 general aviation aircraft violated the temporary flight restriction. NORAD fighter aircraft, including F-16s, were deployed as a “standard precautionary measure to ensure airspace security and establish visual contact with the unresponsive aircraft,” NORAD said in a statement.

In 10 of those instances, fighter aircraft performed tactical intercepts to get the attention of the pilots. During two of those intercepts, flares were dispensed which may have been visible to the public. Those flares were used to ensure pilots saw the NORAD aircraft and to communicate with the pilots, the agency said.

“All 15 situations were safely resolved with the aircraft escorted out of the restricted airspace,” NORAD said. 

During flight restrictions, pilots are expected to pay attention to NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions), which are filed with aviation authorities to notify pilots about airspace restrictions and hazards. During an interception, two fighters approach the plane, with pilots usually only seeing one, according to NORAD. The intent is to identify the plane and try to figure out why it’s in restricted space and encourage them to communicate with air traffic controllers. The fighter jets can also help escort the plane out of the airspace. If that doesn’t work, flares are deployed to get the attention of the pilot. 

The Federal Aviation Administration on Monday said it investigates all flight restriction violations and takes “appropriate action.” The agency said it does not discuss open investigations and referred questions to the U.S. Northern Command and the U.S. Secret Service. The agency said sanctions range from warnings to license suspensions or revocations, based on the circumstances of the violation.

Sunday marked Trump’s first visit to Illinois during his second presidency. He last came to Chicago in July 2024 during a combative interview at the National Association of Black Journalists conference, where he questioned the racial identity of Vice President Kamala Harris and lambasted a moderator’s question about derogatory statements he has made toward the Black community.

news.title: California AG Refuses to Admit His State’s Climate Agenda Has an Affordability Problem
news.text:
Cost of living is the name of the game in politics right now. Prices remain too high, household budgets are stretched thin, and voters are demanding a long-overdue reset. Yet California politicians appear to be operating in a different universe, one where the state’s high costs are not a warning sign, but a point of pride. 

In an interview with POLITICO released Monday, California Attorney General Rob Bonta was asked whether the state’s heavy-handed environmental regulations conflict with voters’ desire for lower costs. Rather than acknowledge the obvious tension, Bonta delivered a word salad worthy of Kamala Harris. He boasted about California’s role as the world’s fourth-largest economy, its so-called protections for workers and consumers, and its environmental initiatives. Bonta’s argument, in effect, was that California is not out of touch, it is simply “leading.”

I think we lead.”REMINDER: California’s climate policies make… pic.twitter.com/0dhgNoJmZv— Steve Guest (@SteveGuest) September 28, 2026

"Aren't you a little bit worried that your climate pursuits seem a little out of touch with everyday Americans?"

"California is going to be California," Bonta said. "And that means leading, that means pushing, that means being on the front foot, that means leading with facts and science. And California has always been a leader. We've led with being the fourth largest economy in the world. We've led with protections for workers and consumers. We've led with our environmental initiatives. We will continue to lead. And oftentimes, we go first and others follow."

"So leading to do something that's important to do and the right thing to do doesn't mean out of touch. It means you're leading. And it means you're inspiring and you're showing the way and you're shining light on a path that we need to go down together," he added. "So no, I don't think we're out of touch. I think we lead. And I think that the next governor of California will have his ability to put his mark on California. I don't expect him to be the same as Governor Newsom. He will be Xavier Becerra. And I look forward to partnering with him and advancing California's including protecting our natural resources and advancing our environmental goals."

In other words, so long as California can claim it is “leading,” whether in environmental mandates, regulatory ambition, or simply the cost of staying afloat, Bonta and the state’s Democrat establishment seem perfectly willing to make the tradeoff on the public’s behalf. Rising utility bills, housing costs, fuel prices, and grocery tabs are apparently just the admission fee for being governed by people who confuse expensive with successful policy.

California may indeed lead the nation in plenty of categories, but it is only a matter of time before the state’s Democratic supermajority squanders the very successes it so consistently cites as proof of its good leadership.

news.title: I spoke to Joe Biden moments after THAT embarrassing meltdown against Trump... I abandoned the party and became a Republican after witnessing the shameless deception of Americans
news.text:
It was the night of June 27, 2024, and Lindy Li could feel her whole body shaking. She wasn't sure if it was intense hunger after a stressful day with no food, or the shock of seeing one of her heroes crumble in front of the entire nation.

The 81-year-old President, Joe Biden, had just put in a devastatingly shambolic debate performance against Donald Trump – the moment his attempt at a second presidential term tanked. Li, a prolific Democratic Party fundraiser, claims to have been one of the first people with whom he spoke on his arrival at the location where party loyalists had been watching the president's dismal showing on big screen TVs.

'I was shaking... like, I cannot believe this happened. I knew he was slowing down, that's no secret, but I didn't know he was going to face plant,' Li told the Daily Mail. 'I didn't know it was going to be an outright collapse. It was just embarrassing [and] painful to watch.'

As an avowed Democratic Party insider, Li, 35, had a front row seat to the implosion of Biden's campaign for re-election and the subsequent ascension of his Vice President Kamala Harris to the ticket, only for her to suffer a crushing defeat to Donald Trump.

Speaking to the President afterwards, she felt sorrow at the diminished figure before her. 'I had so much compassion for him, I didn't mention the debate -- I consoled him,' she told the Daily Mail. '[I felt] love and pity – actual pity – and that is not the feeling you want to have for your President.'

Now, when Li thinks back on what she recalls as an excruciating time, her overwhelming feeling is not compassion and sadness, but anger and guilt about all her friends and contacts who opened their wallets and gave her millions of dollars for what she claims the Democrats always knew was a losing cause.

As she exposes in her new book - Unburdened: A Former Democratic Insider's Shocking Account of Political Power, Betrayal, and Party Collapse, out on Tuesday – the former Liberal fundraiser not only lost faith in her party but switched sides entirely. So disenchanted was she by the millions she claims she saw squandered in behind-the-scenes excesses, the 'cult'-like mentality she alleges was fostered and the Biden family's and closest advisors' seeming desperation to cling to power.

She writes that Biden was 'shamelessness in human form,' while Harris is dismissed as the 'Cackle Queen.'

But perhaps what bites the most is the extent to which she feels she played a part in the deception she said she witnessed behind closed doors: '[People] were donating to the campaign because of their faith in me, and that propelled my need for accountability afterwards, because I felt like it was a personal betrayal.'

Today, Li doesn't hold back on the blame. Some of the most shocking claims in her book relate to what she alleges Democrats – and specifically Harris – spent in donor money on fripperies such as the Vice President's hairstyle, celebrity endorsers and frivolous gift baskets.

Breaking the code of loyalty and openly criticizing the Democratic Party in the aftermath of the November 2024 election defeat, Li switched her allegiance to the Republican Party in December 2024.

Li has earned herself plenty of enemies for such a polarizing move, but she feels like her life has toughened her to the blows she has faced in the past year.

Li was born in China, but when she was two weeks old her parents left her with her grandmother to move to Sheffield, England. She joined them when she was three years old in 1994, spending two years in the UK before relocating again to the United States.

After moving around for her father's job in academia, they settled in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania when Li was nine. Her father transitioned into real estate, making good money and catapulting the family into the upper echelons of Philadelphia society.

'I went to college with billionaires,' she said. 'That's just my life.'

Despite parents who Li said 'very much wanted me to be a traditional East Asian wife,' she was instead drawn to politics. She studied philosophy at Princeton where she was class President for each of her four years at the university.

After graduation, she joined Morgan Stanley as a wealth manager but quit in 2015 at age 25 to run for Congress in Pennsylvania's Democratic primary.

Even though she describes herself as socially conservative, she was swept up in the optimism of the first Obama administration, and it was an automatic assumption among her liberal peers at college that she would join the Democrats.

'I was told the other side consisted of Nazis, so it didn't even compute,' she said.

Her first attempt to run for office in 2016 failed when the signatures for her Pennsylvania candidacy were deemed invalid. Her opponent in the race had challenged her nominating petition, alleging she did not receive the required 1,000 signatures due to invalid signatures – the notary, Li said, had stamped but not signed them. She withdrew from the race.

'I take full responsibility,' she said at the time. 'I understand it is my job to make sure that it's done correctly.

'I've learned my lesson and no one will be able to exploit my weaknesses in the future.' 

And so, in 2018, she tried again. She came sixth in that primary, but she had caught the eye of the Democratic Party for other reasons: She had raised a large sum of money for a 27-year-old candidate with little political experience. Li claimed in media interviews that she raised $600,000 but the Federal Election Committee shows she received just over $168,000.

And so began Li's ascent to the top tiers of Democratic fundraising. Working the phones, schmoozing her contacts in society and businesses and hosting extravagant soirees attended by top Democratic figures on the rooftop pool of her luxury apartment, Li threw herself into the task of getting Biden elected for a second term.

'I wanted to lift him up, I loved him so much,' she said.

That deep loyalty meant that she was among the many insiders who, she claims, initially put on their blinders as Biden's frailty became clear during the second half of his Presidency.

But even as she appeared on TV and social media gushing about the president's competence, she admitted, she was engulfed with a creeping sense that he was ill equipped to lead the nation for a second term.

She also bristled at her own treatment in the party claiming she was pigeonholed into Asian American lobbying groups that she felt little identification with. 'The DNC imprisoned me in a racial silo against my will,' she writes in Unburdened, recalling a Democratic National Convention event at which she was asked to attend alongside a dancing Chinese lion.

Li maintains in her tome that those close to Biden – including his wife Jill and his son Hunter – knew that he did not have the capacity to serve another term but were seduced by their proximity to power and did everything they could to hide his age-related decline.

Both Jill and Hunter have point blank rejected the suggestion they had any sense that Biden was unfit for office, though Jill said in her own memoir that, on seeing her husband's disastrous debate performance she wondered whether he was 'having a stroke,' writing that she had, 'never ever seen Joe like that before or since.'

'The campaign had long since narrowed to a single, obsessive priority: Shielding the fragile ego of one aging leader rather than safeguarding the republic he swore to serve,' Li writes.

While Li also confessed to keeping up the charade immediately after the debate, she appeared on Fox News on July 21, one month after the debate aftermath, saying it was 'not my place to tell President Biden what to do but if he were to step aside, Vice President Kamala Harris would be an excellent candidate.'

Her timing was fortuitous: Later that same day, Biden announced that he was stepping down. Then came what Li sees as the second betrayal: the anointment of Harris to the Presidential ticket without any primary voting process.

Despite an initial swell of optimism, Li claimed that Democratic Party insiders knew Harris was a flawed candidate but rushed to anoint her anyway, given the lack of time until the election and the potential negative optics of overlooking a Black woman for the position. For her part, Li said, it took her only a week to raise $2 million for Harris, whereas it was a full year to bring in $1.1 million for Biden.

Still, she accused the party of 'enthroning a deeply inadequate woman as the spearhead in their battle against Trump and exchanging a cognitively broken man for a cognitive mediocrity.'

Li claimed she was pressured into publicly praising Harris on television and on her social media accounts, as well as keeping the donor money flowing, only to see it squandered on concerts with celebrities, endless goody bags for donors and even, she claimed, $69,000 in styling. In fact, the Daily Mail obtained Harris's campaign filings, which showed she spent $1 billion in her losing bid, including paying $69,000 to crew who worked on a Vogue magazine feature.

'I would get care packages every three weeks, and I knew I was raising the money for it, which is the oddest thing,' Li told the Daily Mail. 'That's my money that they're just blowing on trinkets. Why are you preaching to the converted?'

The Daily Mail has reached out to representatives for Harris for comment.

In the months that followed, Li claimed there were conflicts of interest among top staff and a revolving door of White House staffers into consulting firms that receive the donor money. All the while, she attended a host of DNC events that she described as 'a game of whack-a-celebrity, a bacchanal of self-congratulation and coastal elitism, the smell of uncut money wafting in the air.'

So, when the results came in on November 5, Li said she was devastated but not surprised. Soon after, she started appearing on the TV networks, discussing the flaws in the Harris campaign.

Her friends in the Democratic Party, she claims, swiftly turned on her. Cast into the political wilderness, she finally found acceptance among the conservative pundits and podcasters.

Today, she describes herself as a 'conservative-leaning independent.' While critics allege she is an opportunist happy to do a complete ideological U-turn to be close to power, she insists she is motivated by a desire to fix the country.

Li does not define herself as a member of the MAGA movement despite fundraising Trump's inauguration. She does not support the Iran war and still advocates for environmental protections and gun control.

'I want to be one of the greatest voices in my generation to affect the things that I want to do to ensure, for example, that children aren't getting slaughtered in classrooms and to make sure that everyone's clean air and clean water,' she said.

Despite her evisceration of the Democrats in her book, she believes that they are on track to trounce the Republicans at the midterms in November.

'It's my job to study the American people and how they feel,' she said. 'They are fuming right now. They are hurting, and I hurt with them.'

For now, Li has stepped back from fundraising, given the lack of a candidate she fully supports. But she is keen to remind the political establishment that she and her rolodex still exist, ready to spring into action.

'I do whatever is right for our country, and I'm waiting for a candidate that I can totally support.

'If I wanted to raise five million dollars I could. I know exactly who to call.
news.summary: As an avowed Democratic Party insider, Lindy Li had a front row seat to the implosion of Biden's campaign for re-election and the ascension of his Vice President Kamala Harris to the ticket.

news.title: Heartland Republican calls out 'taxpayer-funded' TV ads in break from Trump
news.text:
Republican congressional candidate Brinker Harding is splitting with the Trump administration regarding its use of taxpayer-funded television campaign advertisements and is stating that Washington should concentrate on those Americans who are having to deal with high costs rather than use public money for political messaging.

“America is $40 trillion dollars in debt, and Nebraskans are struggling to make ends meet. We should be laser focused on spending the taxpayers’ hard earned dollars wisely, not funding political TV advertisements with their money,” Harding said.

“On the Omaha City Council, I balance the city budget every year while ensuring our citizens get the essential services their tax dollars go toward. I will do the same thing in Washington," he added.

Harding is the Republican candidate for Nebraska's 2nd Congressional District, a seat in the Omaha area which is still a competitive district. Although Kamala Harris won the district in the 2024 presidential election, the Republican representative Don Bacon secured re-election with 50.9 per cent of the vote. Bacon is now retiring and is therefore leaving the vacancy to be filled by Harding, who will have to face Democrat Denise Powell and Libertarian Eric Michael Foreman.

The White House is, at the same time, extending a series of television advertisements featuring President Donald Trump, which are funded by the U.S. government.

A 30-second advertisement shown on Fox News and Newsmax displayed images of Trump, highlighted his record on taxes and manufacturing and stated that “America will never be a communist country.” The advertisement included a declaration that it was “Paid for by the U.S. Government,” as reported by The Associated Press.

The White House has described the commercials as public service announcements, stating that they are educational and patriotic and not campaign advertising. Since Trump will not be a candidate in the November election, the advertisements do not directly urge viewers to vote for Republican candidates.

The campaign has come under criticism from members of both political parties. The Republican senator from North Carolina, Thom Tillis, who is not running for re-election, described the advertising as inappropriate, and the Democrats have raised questions as to whether the spending conforms to the federal rules concerning taxpayer-funded publicity or propaganda.

In recent days, the administration has extended the campaign by launching a new advertisement which included footage of Mount Rushmore and extracts from Trump's July 4 speech. According to AdImpact, the amount spent on the first commercial by Friday reached at least $443,000.

Fiscal discipline has been incorporated into Harding's campaign. He stated in a voter guide for the Nebraska Examiner that Congress should cut waste, review the federal programs and return to a more regular budget process.

The fact that he is making his criticism comes while both sides are stressing affordability and household costs in the area in the lead-up to the election on Nov. 3.

news.title: Backlash ensues after the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire calls for assassinations, again
news.text:
The Libertarian Party of New Hampshire is facing backlash after calling for the assassination of “basically every elected Democrat” in the state in a now-deleted X post. 

This wasn’t a first for the LPNH. The group has a history of calling for assassinations of elected officials, and voicing other extreme and divisive rhetoric online that ultimately led to their disaffiliation with the National Libertarian Party. 

In the past, the NHLP has condoned the assassination of Kamala Harris, used its platform to direct homophobic rhetoric at Libertarian presidential nominee Chase Oliver, and openly criticized the national party’s effectiveness. 

The national party cut ties with the LPNH in May, due to the “unfortunate culmination of years of behavior in violation of the Libertarian Party’s platform,” Libertarian National Committee Chair Evan McMahon said in a statement posted on social media. 

The Libertarian Party Judicial Committee later unanimously rejected LPNH’s appeal and the national party now recognizes the Granite State Libertarian Party as its New Hampshire affiliate. 

In a statement regarding LPNH’s most recent statement, the national party said calling for violence goes against the party’s ideals. 

“The Non-Aggression Principle is a fundamental core of libertarianism,” the party said on social media. “It is not optional, and it is central to what our party stands for.”

Many New Hampshire Democrats, and some Republicans, took to social media to voice their disapproval of LPNH’s post. 

“Rhetoric calling for political assassination has no place in New Hampshire or our country — something we should all be able to agree on regardless of our political beliefs,” U.S. Rep. Chris Pappas, who is currently running for Senate in New Hampshire, said in a statement. “We work out our differences through the democratic process where we engage in civil debate and seek common ground whenever possible.” 

U.S. Rep Maggie Goodlander called on the New Hampshire Attorney General and federal law enforcement to investigate the threat. 

“I condemn, with every fiber of my being, the threats of and calls for murder from the Libertarian Party of New Hampshire,” she said on social media. “…You can disagree with someone as deeply as humanly possible. But in the United States of America you cannot call for their killing and go unpunished.” 

Lily Tang Williams, a Republican congressional nominee challenging Goodlander, condemned LPNH’s promotion of political violence. 

“Political violence has no place in America — period,” she said in a statement. “As someone who survived an oppressive communist regime where political violence was common, I know we should never take for granted our ability to settle disagreements through free speech, peaceful debate, and elections.” 

Days after the controversial post was made, LPNH chair Jeremy Kauffman posted a screenshot showing that the LPNH account had been temporarily locked for a week or more for breaking X’s rules. 

“It remains a major asymmetry that communists can openly argue for mass enslavement, but patriots cannot advocate for self-defense,” Kauffman said in regards to LPNH’s temporary suspension. 

LPNH said on social media earlier this month it offered to turn over all of its assets to the Granite State Libertarian Party, including its social media account, but the offer was rejected by the national party. 

The national Libertarian party leadership team said it is “reviewing all legal options to protect the Party’s brand of freedom, peace, and prosperity,” according to the Boston Globe.
news.summary:
The group's prior divisive rhetoric ultimately led to their disaffiliation with the National Libertarian Party.

news.title: Trump and GOP See Reversal With Latinos in 2 Strongholds Ahead of Midterms
news.text: Hispanic voters in South Texas and South Florida are showing signs of moving away from President Donald Trump and the Republican Party, just five weeks before the midterm elections. The two regions were key to Trump's gains with Latino voters in 2024, when he made major inroads in heavily Hispanic areas of both states. Now, Republican-held House seats in South Texas and South Florida are becoming more competitive, while the Texas U.S. Senate race has also tightened. For Democrats, the shift has raised hopes of winning a statewide election in Texas for the first time since 1994. The Cook Political Report, widely considered the industry standard for nonpartisan race ratings, moved three Florida House races and three Texas House races toward Democrats, including Texas' 9th Congressional District, which had long been considered solidly Republican. While the two electorates are different, political strategists who track Latino voters told Newsweek they are responding to many of the same concerns. The Latino Problem for the GOP in Texas A survey of Hispanic likely voters in Texas conducted for the Cook Political Report and TelevisaUnivision found Trump's job approval at 33 percent, two years after he carried Texas Hispanics by 10 percentage points. Republican Senator Ted Cruz won the group by 3 points in 2024. Texas state Representative James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee, leads Republican Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton 63 percent to 30 percent among Hispanic voters, including 73 percent of self-described independents. In the governor's race, Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa leads Republican Governor Greg Abbott 60 percent to 33 percent. Abbott won 40 percent of Hispanics in 2022. Much of the movement comes from Trump voters. Eighteen percent of Texas Hispanics who backed him in 2024 disapprove of his performance, 19 percent support Talarico over Paxton and 22 percent do not back a Republican in a generic House matchup. Mike Madrid, a longtime Republican strategist and author of The Latino Century, said Washington misread what happened in 2024. "People, I think, broadly are failing to understand that the Latino vote is the largest swing vote in America," Madrid told Newsweek. "Most people were thinking it was part of this permanent realignment. A lot of people who understand the Latino vote were saying it's not that at all." Immigration enforcement is also a drag. Nearly two-thirds of respondents said they would be less likely to vote for a candidate who supports Trump's deportation policy, and 61 percent view Immigration and Customs Enforcement unfavorably. Voters still ranked the economy as their top concern by roughly 2-to-1 over immigration. Every public poll of the race conducted in September has shown Talarico ahead, most within the margin of error. Newsweek reached out to the Paxton and Talarico campaigns for comment Monday. South Texas House Races Tighten as Latino Voters Shift On September 25, Cook moved three Texas House races toward Democrats: the 15th District from Lean Republican to Toss-Up, the 35th from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, and the 9th from Solid Republican to Likely Republican. Only the 15th is in the Rio Grande Valley, though Cook's poll also sampled voters in the Democratic-held 28th and 34th districts, both of which Texas Republicans redrew last year to make them more favorable to the GOP. But the pressure is visible there. Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer with two Latin Grammy Awards and broad name recognition across South Texas, is challenging Republican Representative Monica De La Cruz in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024. A Texas Southern University poll puts Pulido ahead 50 percent to 45 percent. Madrid, who recently traveled to South Texas, said voters there described specific grievances. He pointed to the administration's moves on Argentine beef in a region built on ranching. "This is cattle-ranching country," he said. "He's literally poking the stick in the eye of fifth-generation Hispanic cattle ranchers. It's not like an academic discussion or a debate. He's directly attacking their businesses." In the 28th District, Democratic Representative Henry Cuellar faces Tano Tijerina, a Webb County judge who switched from Democrat to Republican and won the GOP primary decisively. Trump won the district by 10 points under the new map. Cook rated the race Lean Democratic after Trump's pardon in December 2025 ended the federal bribery case against Cuellar. Coverage in recent months has focused on the race tightening, with Trump criticizing Cuellar while openly backing Tijerina. The 34th District, which covers the Brownsville-McAllen area, is also roughly Trump +10 under the new lines. There, Democratic Representative Vicente Gonzalez faces Republican Eric Flores, a former assistant U.S. attorney. No independent general-election poll of the race has been published. An NRCC poll in late April had Flores ahead 41 percent to 40 percent, and a mid-June Ragnar Research poll had him up 44 percent to 41 percent. Cook and Sabato's Crystal Ball rate it a Toss-Up. What Polling Shows in the Florida Races After Cook's Shift If any place has rewarded the Republican Party, and Trump in particular, for courting Hispanic voters, it is South Florida. In 2016, Hillary Clinton won Miami-Dade County by 29 points. Four years later, Joe Biden carried it by just 7. In 2024, Trump became the first Republican presidential candidate since 1988 to win the county, where roughly 71 percent of the 2.8 million residents are Hispanic. He beat Kamala Harris there by 11 points, and an NBC exit poll found that he won 58 percent of the Latino vote statewide. The shift was built largely on Cuban and Venezuelan American voters, many of whom fled leftist governments and have long seen the GOP as their political home. Those are the voters Republicans now risk losing. On September 25, Cook moved three Florida House races toward Democrats: the 27th and 13th districts from Likely Republican to Lean Republican, and the 22nd from Lean Republican to Toss-Up. Republican Representative Maria Elvira Salazar's 27th District, which covers Miami, Coral Gables, Palmetto Bay and Cutler Bay, is the one most tied to Latino voters. Almost three in four residents are Latino. Cook cited recent polls and a Hispanic backlash against the Trump administration that it said forced Salazar to play defense. The race has escalated in recent days. After Salazar's ad criticizing Trump's immigration enforcement, the president shared at least 14 posts from other users attacking her on Truth Social. She has not directly responded to his weekend posts. Newsweek reached out to Salazar for comment Monday. An internal poll for her Democratic challenger, former CBS Miami anchor Eliott Rodriguez, found the two tied at 45 percent once undecided voters were asked. The same survey found Trump 10 points underwater in the district, with 54 percent disapproving of his job performance. Forty-four percent said Salazar deserves reelection, and 47 percent said they would prefer someone new. The poll was conducted by Bendixen & Amandi International, which works for Rodriguez's campaign. Eduardo Gamarra, a political science professor at Florida International University who publishes a weekly tracking report on the Latino vote in Florida, told Newsweek that his report had flagged Salazar's district as competitive for the first time this cycle. "I live there. I'm already seeing a lot more negative commentary about her online than I was a week ago," he said. The newly drawn 22nd District stretches across parts of western Broward and Palm Beach counties and includes Hendry and Collier counties. The old district backed Trump 55 percent to 44 percent in 2024 after voting for Joe Biden 51 percent to 48 percent in 2020. Democrat Pia Dandiya is running against Republican Casey Askar. In the Tampa Bay-area 13th District, Democrat Leela Gray leads Republican Representative Anna Paulina Luna 51 percent to 46 percent in a House Majority PAC poll conducted by Hart Research Associates. An internal poll conducted for Luna by Fabrizio, Lee & Associates in August showed her leading by 8 points, a sign of how much the race has shifted in recent polling. What Other Polls Say About Latino Voters Other surveys point the same direction. A Pew Research Center survey in April found that 66 percent of Latino Trump voters approve of his job performance, down 27 percentage points since the start of his second term in January 2025. A New York Times/Siena poll conducted September 8-13 places Trump's approval among Hispanic voters at 26 percent. In Texas, a separate UnidosUS poll found that 54 percent of Latino voters surveyed across five competitive districts planned to support the Democratic candidate, compared with 27 percent for the Republican. The same polls carry warnings for Democrats. Texas Hispanic voters in the Cook survey preferred Republican messaging on transgender athletes over a progressive alternative by more than 20 points, though few named it as a top issue. In Florida, the UnidosUS poll found that dissatisfaction with Trump is not translating into support for Democratic candidates in the two marquee races on the statewide ballot. Among Hispanic voters in Florida, Republican Senator Ashley Moody led Democratic state Representative Angie Nixon 40 percent to 32 percent, while in the governor's race, Republican Representative Byron Donalds led Democrat David Jolly, a former GOP congressman, 40 percent to 33 percent. More than one-quarter of respondents were undecided in each race. "This is 100 percent about the Republicans," Madrid told Newsweek. "Not that the Democrats are doing anything right. It's that the Republicans are doing everything wrong." Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Dave Siminoff.
news.summary: Hispanic voters in South Texas and South Florida are showing signs of moving away from President Donald Trump.

news.title: Kamala Harris Brutally Mocked as Ex-Veep Hits Midterm Campaign Trail — as Critics Say She's 'Still Giving a Word Salad Answer for Everything
news.text:
Democrats in Michigan have little enthusiasm for former Vice President Kamala Harris and her "word salad," with some critics saying, once more, that she comes off as confusing or insincere, RadarOnline can report.

Harris is making stops in key midterm battlegrounds, including an appearance in Michigan alongside Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.Kamala Harris' Latest 'Word Salad'She is also scheduled to campaign for Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford.

At a maternal and infant health center, Harris spoke about what "black people and black birthing people need in order to move themselves forward." She linked attacks on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) to threats against maternal care for Black women.

"[An attack on DEI] is an attack by definition on maternal care, including the need to protect Black women in connection with their pregnancy, childbirth and postpartum care," Harris said.

The connection between the two topics was not explained, prompting one anonymous Democratic operative to tell The New York Post she was saying "a whole lot of word salad."Kamala Harris Making a Comeback?Harris has not decided whether she will run for president in 2028, but her midterm activity is fueling speculation that she is keeping the option open. 

The Associated Press reported that she is actively campaigning for Democratic candidates in Michigan, Nevada and Georgia as she considers a potential 2028 bid.

As Radar previously reported, Gov. Gavin Newsom is also being discussed as a potential 2028 candidate. Her name remains prominent in early 2028 Democratic preference polling. 

The RealClearPolitics average through September 21 has Harris at 24.9 percent, followed by Newsom at 14 percent, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg at 12.8 percent, and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez at 10.7 percent.Kansas Dem Candidate's Plea to Kamala Harris: 'Don’t Come'Meanwhile, some Democrats have questioned her value as a surrogate. 

Kansas Senate candidate Pastor Adam Hamilton said on State of Play with Peter Alexander on September 23 that Harris would not help his campaign and preferred she stay away.

Hamilton said he and Harris are ideologically different and argued that her appearance could hurt his chances with undecided voters and Republicans who are frustrated with President Trump's policies and could be considering voting Democratic.

"No offense intended for her, but she would not be a help to me," Hamilton told Alexander. "We are a different kind of Democrat, and the national Democrats, some of the leaders, do not represent where the people in Kansas are."Old GaffesHarris' choice of words and phrases has drawn criticism throughout her vice presidency and her 2024 presidential campaign.

One of the most memorable lines from her 2024 campaign came in Pittsburgh on September 2, 2024, when she said, "We have dreams. We can see what is possible, unburdened by what has been. We have aspirations. We have ambitions, and the system that is a good system is one that supports that and allows people the opportunity to go where they can see and imagine themselves to be."

In a January 2022 interview with NBC's Today, Harris was asked whether it was time to change the Biden administration’s COVID-19 strategy.

"It is time for us to do what we have been doing. And that time is every day," she said before discussing efforts to slow the spread of the virus.

On August 2, 2024, while discussing a prisoner exchange that brought three detained Americans home from Russia, Harris said on CNN it was "an extraordinary testament to the importance of having a president who understands the power of diplomacy and understands the strength that rests in understanding the significance of diplomacy and strengthening alliances."
news.summary: Kamala Harris faces renewed criticism over her speaking style as she returns to the midterm campaign trail for Democratic candidates in Michigan, Georgia and Nevada.
news.author: Christian Spencer

news.title: Rocker Michael Stipe Holding Major NYC Fundraiser for Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed
news.text:
R.E.M. frontman Michael Stipe is set to help host a massive fundraiser in Manhattan for Michigan Democrat U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, reports say.

The big event will be held on the Bowery on October 5, an advanced flyer for the fundraiser notes, according to the New York Post.

Stipe will be joined by New York jeweler Alexis Bittar, Democrat House candidate Brad Lander, ex-Congressman Jamaal Bowman, and Brooklyn Councilman Chi Osse.

Socialist New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s close campaign aides, political strategists Andrew Bard Esptein and Zara Rahim, are also members of the hosting group.

Bard Esptein reportedly told the media that he has joined the El-Sayed event because the Michigan Democrat is a “candidate I believe in.”

Tickets cost from between $250 for the lowest level to $57,800 for the top tier of donors.

The flyer works to take the edge off El-Sayed Muslim and radical left-wing background by calling him a “Michigan native running to make government work for ALL of us.”

R.E.M.’s Stipe has stumped for far-left candidates in the past. Back in 2016, for instance, he campaigned for socialist U.S. Senator Bernie Sanders in his last losing campaign for the Democrat nomination for president.

He also supported Kamala Harris in 2024 and was one of many in the entertainment industry to urge Joe Biden to step down from running against Donald Trump that year.
